sources.title: Crypto giant Binance attempting to recover $6.3bn stolen in hack linked to North Korea - BBC
passages: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist .
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor.
The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.

While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person.
Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."

Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.

The firm said $3bn of its stolen digital assets had been secured - but many were still in the hands of unidentified hackers. It initially thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider. Several analytics firms have linked the hack, which eclipses a $1.5bn (£1.12bn) heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025, to a North Korean hacking unit. The US Secret Service said it was "working around the clock" "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover" stolen funds. America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI. While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort. The hack also involved some US-linked assets, such as stablecoins Tether and Circle – cryptocurrencies pegged to the dollar. Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss". It had initially suspended all deposits and withdrawals - but then said in an update that "deposits remain unaffected". Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person. Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach." Teng also describes how the hackers used "a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate". Initially, the company had indicated the breach "may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop" but later statements have pointed to a broader breach. In a later update, the firm said it had "set aside" more than $6.34B in company funds to cover the stolen assets and was "actively buying" a range of crypto tokens. The Binance hack spooked cryptocurrency markets on Friday. The price of Bitcoin was down 5% to $76,800 in Friday afternoon trading in New York. Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase was down 12% as investors also reacted to earnings results in which the firm reported revenue slightly below expectations. Robinhood, a financial services company that trades in cryptocurrency, was down 7.8%. Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide. The company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets under its custody. Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world. Meanwhile, AI-powered investigations company TRM Labs said that several elements of the attack resembled earlier North Korean-linked incidents, including the Bybit hack. In the last five years the crypto industry has been beset by enormous losses from hackers. Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.

The latest update marks progress from the exchange's previous disclosure that it had covered approximately 80% of the stolen assets.
Binance said the remaining tokens were less liquid, making them more difficult to source and replace.

The exchange also said it was working to restore withdrawals by Sunday.
Binance's commitment to make users whole and its plan to resume withdrawals are key steps in its effort to restore confidence following the attack.

sources.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack - BBC
passages: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
Binance has been hit by what could be the biggest crypto hack ever - here's what we know so far

Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack. The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services. Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits. Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said. North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks. Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.

Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.

Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has replaced 90 per cent of the ⁠amount stolen after a record $6.3 billion (€5.63 billion) hack of its platform by a group the FBI identified as being backed by North Korea . The remaining 10 per cent of tokens are less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday. Co-chief executive Richard Teng said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10 per cent” and that “users will not bear the financial impact of this incident”. Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said on Sunday that some had resumed and would be rolled out in phases to ensure stability. The announcement came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack. TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. “The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement. The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services. It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets”. [ Central Bank fines Irish-based unit of crypto giant Coinbase €3.3m Opens in new window ] Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the losses. [ New Government investment accounts could generate up to €400m in fees for banks Opens in new window ] “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said. The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its Futures Insurance Fund and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said ​on X. The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. Bitcoin plunged nearly 5 per cent after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6 per cent and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 per cent. coreStoryFacts.text: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has frozen around half of the funds stolen in a "complex" hack, after $6.3bn (£4.7bn) was accessed in what is believed to be a record heist .
Chainalysis, a crypto analytics firm, said it had "high confidence" that a North Korean is linked to the hack.
Several experts have warned customers not to regard Binance's promise to cover losses as legally binding and said they may need to pursue litigation to recover them.
In nearly all cases investigators have blamed hackers from North Korea, pointing to the infamous Lazarus Group - also know as TraderTraitor.
The names refer to clusters of cyber criminals accused of working directly for the regime.
North Korea is an impoverished country with very little industry and heavy international sanctions and experts say the regime uses cyber crime as a way to bring money in.
Who could be behind the Binance hack and what we know so far
Binance, which was founded in China in 2017, allows users to trade digital assets and is estimated to have more than 300 million registered users worldwide.
A lot of the fear right now from Binance users - and the crypto industry at large - is whether or not Binance will actually be capable of covering this enormous financial loss.

America's lead federal agency for investigating financial crimes added that it would "identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice", while Binance also said it was working with the FBI.

While Binance said its US-facing exchange was unaffected, the US would still have jurisdiction to investigate the hack and help track down stolen funds - an effort which generally involves a global law enforcement effort.
Binance told its users "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss".
Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said: "This was not carried out by one person.
Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach."

Daniel Tunkel, of the London-based Edwin Coe law firm, said that would "come down to what [customers] have been promised in their contracts", and "where Binance can be sued for non-performance, if it comes to it".
Binance has been subject of regulatory scrutiny around the world.

But crypto history watchers have been pointing out online that this is exactly the kind of message that FTX CEO Sam Bankman-Fried gave before his crypto exchange collapsed in 2022, leading to huge losses for customers and the industry.
The company has said repeatedly that customer funds will be covered and that the firm is strong enough to weather the storm.

The incident has sent shockwaves through the cryptocurrency industry.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Bitcoin cuts some losses, but falls below $77k after Binance hit with $6.3B hack
The latest update marks progress from the exchange's previous disclosure that it had covered approximately 80% of the stolen assets.
Binance said the remaining tokens were less liquid, making them more difficult to source and replace.

The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday. In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack. It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack. The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services. Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits. Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said. The remaining 10 per cent of tokens are less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday. Co-chief executive Richard Teng said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10 per cent” and that “users will not bear the financial impact of this incident”. Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said on Sunday that some had resumed and would be rolled out in phases to ensure stability. The announcement came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack. TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. “The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement. The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services. It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets”. [ Central Bank fines Irish-based unit of crypto giant Coinbase €3.3m Opens in new window ] Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the losses. [ New Government investment accounts could generate up to €400m in fees for banks Opens in new window ] “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said. The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its Futures Insurance Fund and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said ​on X. The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. Bitcoin plunged nearly 5 per cent after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6 per cent and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 per cent. The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue. – Guardian From maternity leave to remote working: Submit your work-related questions here Listen to Inside Business podcast for a look at business and economics from an Irish perspective Get the latest business news and commentary from our expert business team in your inbox every weekday morning

sources.title: AI boom hits a wall on Wall Street as OpenAI cuts fundraising target while Meta gets a credit warning over its cash flow, spending and monetization - Yahoo Finance
passages: Quarterly earnings reports from hyperscalers this week spooked investors.
Alphabet saw its cash flow sink deeper into negative territory in the third quarter, with the Google parent also joining Meta and Amazon in charging ahead with massive spending plans.
On Thursday, Alphabet fell about 12%, its worst day on record.
The funding round was also upstaged by Anthropic, according to the report, as OpenAI's arch-rival prepares to go public next month.
Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta's capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there.
At the same time, OpenAI was seeking more capital just as other AI giants tapped financial markets heavily.
This past week alone, Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in a bond sale.
Following a brutal selloff in tech stocks over the past week, OpenAI slashed the target on its latest fundraising round to $20 billion from $30 billion, sources told the Financial Times .
That also cut its expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion.

The prospect of hyperscalers continuing to hemorrhage funds was too much for S&P Global, which cut its outlook on Meta to "negative" from "stable" late Friday, citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around capital expenditure ​plans.
The credit ratings agency maintained Meta at AA- but warned ⁠the social media leader's leverage could top 1.0x as soon as 2027, which is the downgrade threshold for the current rating.
That's up from about 0.1x in 2025 and primarily reflects its strategy of leasing data center capacity rather than from its debt issuance.

The bearish environment on Wall Street also comes as rising bond yields have sent borrowing costs sharply higher, the political backlash against data centers is expected to help Democrats retake Congress, and the Iran war could re-escalate after midterm elections.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Microsoft reported strong cloud growth and stayed cash flow positive, though it said its capital spending will accelerate, while AI chip maker SK Hynix blew away earnings forecasts.

In a statement to Fortune , a Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with S&P's assessment of its AI monetization capabilities, pointing to "significant product and business opportunities" ahead.
"Meta is already delivering stronger engagement, better recommendations, and greater returns for businesses as a result of AI investments," the spokesperson continued.

"We believe the technology and infrastructure we're building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone."
Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added.
OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

Microsoft reported strong cloud growth and stayed cash flow positive, though it said its capital spending will accelerate, while AI chip maker SK Hynix blew away earnings forecasts. But the narrative had already turned bearish, especially after AI debt fears sent shares and bonds of "neocloud" companies tumbling earlier this month. At the same time, OpenAI was seeking more capital just as other AI giants tapped financial markets heavily. This past week alone, Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in a bond sale. That's up from about 0.1x in 2025 and primarily reflects its strategy of leasing data center capacity rather than from its debt issuance. Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta's capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there. As a result, it expects free operating cash flow to remain negative: -$22 billion this year, -$71 billion in 2027, and -$39 billion in 2028. Of course, other hyperscalers are spending heavily and running cash deficits, but S&P also said Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers. "While we believe the company intends to monetize these investments via improved advertising tools that support faster ad revenue growth, as well as from the development of new revenue streams stemming from its introduction of agentic apps such as Muse, it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years," S&P said. Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added. In a statement to Fortune , a Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with S&P's assessment of its AI monetization capabilities, pointing to "significant product and business opportunities" ahead. "Meta is already delivering stronger engagement, better recommendations, and greater returns for businesses as a result of AI investments," the spokesperson continued. "We believe the technology and infrastructure we're building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone." The bearish environment on Wall Street also comes as rising bond yields have sent borrowing costs sharply higher, the political backlash against data centers is expected to help Democrats retake Congress, and the Iran war could re-escalate after midterm elections. Still, some bullish voices aren't convinced the AI boom is about to go bust, and even think some retrenchment is a good thing . According to market veteran Ed Yardeni, the AI investment boom faces financial, physical, and political constraints. If any of these constraints worsen, stocks could dive further, especially considering that AI is now a major driver of corporate earnings and GDP growth, he said in a note this week. "However, we view these constraints as healthy for the durability of the AI boom!" he added. For example, if the supply of capital doesn't flow as easily, it could lead to more efficient allocation, lowering the risk of overinvestment. Yardeni expects hyperscalers to retain access to financing—thanks to their strong balance sheets—and keep spending. In his view, it all comes down to the U.S. economy, which he said has performed remarkably well over the past few decades. Even the midterm elections are unlikely to derail it, regardless of which party controls Congress. "Further AI jitters therefore could set up buying opportunities rather than signal the end of the boom," he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Microsoft reported strong cloud growth and stayed cash flow positive, though it said its capital spending will accelerate, while AI chip maker SK Hynix blew away earnings forecasts.

Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added.
OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

extraction.body: TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom. But now there is growing uncertainty around just how easily more money can be obtained – and how much of it will be paid back. Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave. Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations. Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s. At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI. The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects. The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out. Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines. The spread, or extra premium that investors demand to put their money into risky AI debt investments, has shot up more than 50 per cent over the past six months, according to Barclays, the investment bank. “The market is on a knife’s edge everywhere,” said Alexandra Coleman, founder of Azraq, a data centre risk researcher. A lot is riding on the continuation of the borrowing binge. Every week lately, economists, banks and private equity firms project higher and higher amounts of debt that they say will be needed to finance the AI systems that their boosters assert will run the world in a few years. Virtually every major mutual fund company, insurer and private equity firm has been buying up the AI debt, to say nothing of the scores of individual investors who have poured money into skyrocketing AI companies. Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally. The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals. Investors have also sold out of some these companies’ existing debt, though the drop in bond prices has been less steep than for CoreWeave. CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description. Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork. First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips. Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more. CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame. The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around. Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire. A CoreWeave spokesperson, Lia Davis, said the company disagreed with the WeWork comparison. “The complexity of our financing reflects discipline, which is a point of pride for us,” she said in a statement. Another worry is the growing number of US data-centre projects being delayed by permitting issues or, in some cases, falling through. Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. In 2025, the company easily borrowed US$38 billion from a group of banks to build, with the help of project developers, a pair of data centres, one in Texas and another on about 809 hectares of farmland in Port Washington, Wisconsin. Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028. Aterio, a data centre researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centres would start operating before 2029. That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan. Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico. The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power. Some of the US$18 billion in debt tied to the project has recently sold at steep discounts, roughly US$0.80 on the US dollar, according to two people familiar with the trades. SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI. The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more. To get that money, Son sold off most of SoftBank’s holdings of Nvidia and T-Mobile and took out loans against his stake in chip designer Arm Holdings. In 2026, Son invested again. On Oct 1, SoftBank completed another US$30 billion investment in OpenAI. Before doing so, in late September the company raised a record US$11 billion in debt at interest rates of nearly 10 per cent. In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed. “The assets we’ve owned have increased significantly,” Clavel said in an interview. The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked. It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt. At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000. Some investors see a potential silver lining to the troubles. John Lloyd, the global head of multisector and corporate credit at asset manager Janus Henderson, said slowing down the financing for projects “makes existing projects and existing AI infrastructure even more valuable.” NYTIMES

CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description. Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.

First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips. Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more. CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future. Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.

A CoreWeave spokesperson, Lia Davis, said the company disagreed with the WeWork comparison. “The complexity of our financing reflects discipline, which is a point of pride for us,” she said in a statement.
Another worry is the growing number of US data-centre projects being delayed by permitting issues or, in some cases, falling through.

Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects. In 2025, the company easily borrowed US$38 billion from a group of banks to build, with the help of project developers, a pair of data centres, one in Texas and another on about 809 hectares of farmland in Port Washington, Wisconsin.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
Aterio, a data centre researcher, said it was looking less likely that Project Lighthouse’s four data centres would start operating before 2029.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due. Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.

Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico. The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.
Some of the US$18 billion in debt tied to the project has recently sold at steep discounts, roughly US$0.80 on the US dollar, according to two people familiar with the trades.

SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI. The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
To get that money, Son sold off most of SoftBank’s holdings of Nvidia and T-Mobile and took out loans against his stake in chip designer Arm Holdings.

“The assets we’ve owned have increased significantly,” Clavel said in an interview.

The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked. It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt. At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.

Some investors see a potential silver lining to the troubles. John Lloyd, the global head of multisector and corporate credit at asset manager Janus Henderson, said slowing down the financing for projects “makes existing projects and existing AI infrastructure even more valuable.” NYTIMES

Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta's capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there. As a result, it expects free operating cash flow to remain negative: -$22 billion this year, -$71 billion in 2027, and -$39 billion in 2028. Of course, other hyperscalers are spending heavily and running cash deficits, but S&P also said Meta's ability to monetize its AI investments is more limited than that of its peers. "While we believe the company intends to monetize these investments via improved advertising tools that support faster ad revenue growth, as well as from the development of new revenue streams stemming from its introduction of agentic apps such as Muse, it is unclear when these revenue streams will generate material contributions that exceed their rising costs over the next few years," S&P said. Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added. According to market veteran Ed Yardeni, the AI investment boom faces financial, physical, and political constraints. If any of these constraints worsen, stocks could dive further, especially considering that AI is now a major driver of corporate earnings and GDP growth, he said in a note this week. For example, if the supply of capital doesn't flow as easily, it could lead to more efficient allocation, lowering the risk of overinvestment. "Further AI jitters therefore could set up buying opportunities rather than signal the end of the boom," he said. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

sources.title: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom

extraction.body: Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down. Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips. Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns. The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again. A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027. Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it. Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday. Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week. Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank . It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year. Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand. These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. The concern is already showing up in stock prices and company cash flows. Investors who once treated large AI outlays as a sign of confidence are now weighing debt, negative free cash flow and whether the investments will generate enough returns.

The companies are expanding infrastructure to meet strong demand for AI computing. But the cost of building that capacity is rising while some core businesses face pressure from AI products that could alter how they make money.

Alphabet offered a clear example this week. Google’s parent reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, while quarterly capital spending rose to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year and said spending should continue rising in 2027.

At the same time, Google’s AI Mode chatbot is built into Search, the company’s major advertising business. Search advertising accounts for roughly half of Alphabet’s revenue, but growth slowed to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. The company is investing heavily in AI technology that could put pressure on the search business funding that investment.

sources.title: Cracks emerge in AI borrowing boom as CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank debt worries grow - The Business Times
passages: The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI. The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects. The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday. The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5bn Bybit hack last year. The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum . The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.” On Thursday, $6.3bn in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack. The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed. Binance promised it would cover all losses from company funds and allow clients to trade again within days. Binance has a $1​bn bitcoin reserve fund designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that the company owned SpaceX shares worth more than $1bn. Binance's other co-CEO, Richard Teng, said in a post ​on X that the breach was a "complex attack" that was not carried out by one person and included a compromised laptop as well as malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity as it ⁠went along, "making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate." The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. "Rest assured that ​we are working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368, and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilized. Bitcoin last stood ​at $76,447 and ether at $2,226. Binance's BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at $696. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. "This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act.
“Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.”

In a statement , the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month )

Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.”

Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act.
“Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.”

In a statement , the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month )

Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.”

A federal judge in Mississippi has rejected an effort by the Trump administration to shut down a lawsuit brought by the NAACP against Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, allowing a closely watched environmental justice case to continue. The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act. The plant supplies power to xAI’s massive Colossus 2 data center, which supports the company’s artificial intelligence operations. The case has drawn attention because of the plant’s location near predominantly Black communities in North Mississippi and South Memphis. Reuters previously reported that pollution tied to the project has raised concerns about whether the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is placing disproportionate environmental burdens on Black neighborhoods. The Trump administration, acting through the Environmental Protection Agency, sought to intervene in the case and argued that the EPA had the authority to terminate the lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown disagreed with that position Monday. Brown ruled that the EPA could participate in the case, but said nothing in the Clean Air Act gives the agency the power to unilaterally dismiss a citizen lawsuit simply because it has intervened. The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved. The lawsuit was originally filed in April. At the time, the NAACP accused xAI of operating dozens of methane gas turbines without the required permits, effectively creating a private power plant to meet the enormous energy demands of its data center. The organization has argued that nearby residents should not have to bear the health and environmental costs of the company’s rapid expansion. The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution. The organization is being represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice. The legal fight comes as communities across the country begin confronting the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, and developers are increasingly turning to on-site power generation to meet demand. That growth has prompted new questions about air quality, energy use and how quickly environmental regulations can keep pace with the AI boom. For the NAACP, the case is about more than one data center. It is part of a broader argument that Black communities should not be expected to absorb additional pollution in the name of technological progress, particularly when those communities have historically faced disproportionate exposure to industrial development and poor air quality. The judge’s ruling does not determine whether xAI violated environmental law. That question still has to be resolved in court. What it does mean is that the NAACP will be allowed to continue pressing its case.

extraction.body: A federal judge just handed the NAACP a major victory in its fight against xAI, allowing a lawsuit alleging Clean Air Act violations at the company's data center to move forward. With AI data centers consuming unprecedented amounts of energy and requiring extensive cooling systems, the ruling could reshape how tech companies approach regulatory compliance. The legal battle puts xAI, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence venture, squarely in the crosshairs of environmental justice advocates who argue the company's data center operations violate federal clean air standards. The judge's decision to let the case proceed past preliminary motions means xAI will now face discovery and potentially a trial on the merits of the NAACP's claims. Just last week, SpaceX closed a massive $40 billion debt deal to purchase GPUs for AI infrastructure, underscoring the breakneck pace of expansion across Musk's technology empire. That infrastructure buildout requires enormous data centers with corresponding energy demands and environmental footprints. The NAACP's lawsuit centers on allegations that xAI's data center operations produce air pollution that exceeds Clean Air Act thresholds without proper permitting or mitigation measures. Environmental advocates have increasingly raised concerns about the energy intensity of AI model training and inference, which requires thousands of high-powered chips running continuously in facilities that generate substantial heat and emissions. Data centers have become flashpoints in communities across the country as residents push back against facilities they see as bringing pollution, noise, and strain on local power grids without commensurate benefits. The judge's ruling doesn't determine the merits of the NAACP's claims, but it does mean the organization cleared the initial hurdles to proceed with litigation. That's significant because tech companies often succeed in getting environmental lawsuits dismissed on procedural grounds before reaching the substance of the allegations. For xAI, the lawsuit adds regulatory uncertainty at a crucial moment. The company competes with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in the race to build more powerful AI systems, a competition that requires massive infrastructure investments. Companies have announced plans for dozens of new data centers to support AI workloads, often in regions offering tax incentives or cheap power. Legal experts say the case could establish important precedents about what level of environmental review and permitting AI data centers require. The Clean Air Act includes provisions for reviewing major new sources of pollution and protecting communities disproportionately affected by environmental hazards, both potentially relevant to large-scale AI infrastructure. The lawsuit also highlights tensions within Musk's broader business empire. The company's rapid growth has occasionally outpaced its ability to navigate complex regulatory frameworks. The case now moves into discovery, where the NAACP will have the opportunity to gather evidence about xAI's operations, emissions, and compliance with air quality standards. That process could reveal new details about how the company manages the environmental impacts of its data center operations and whether it obtained necessary permits before beginning operations. For the NAACP, the ruling represents validation of its strategy to use environmental law as a tool for protecting communities from the potential harms of AI infrastructure expansion. The organization has increasingly focused on technology policy issues, recognizing that decisions about where to locate data centers and other facilities have significant equity implications. The judge's decision to let this lawsuit proceed signals that AI companies can't assume their infrastructure expansion will face only technical and financial hurdles. As xAI and its rivals pour billions into data centers, they'll need to navigate not just the engineering challenges of training massive models, but also the regulatory and legal frameworks designed to protect air quality and environmental justice.

Today, the NAACP filed a request for a preliminary injunction to stop unpermitted air pollution from an illegal power plant built by Elon Musk’s company, xAI, and its subsidiary, MZX Tech. The unpermitted power plant, which is located in Southaven, Mississippi, powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data center in Memphis.
This request follows the organization’s Clean Air Act enforcement lawsuit filed last month . The NAACP is represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice in the case.

In February, the NAACP notified xAI and its subsidiary that their personal power plant consisting of 27 gas-fired turbines violated the Clean Air Act and put the health of local communities at risk. But instead of fixing these problems and complying with federal law, the tech companies did the opposite: they brought six additional gas turbines on site, bringing the total number of turbines at the power plant to 33. These six new turbines — which on their own would be considered a major source of pollution under the Clean Air Act — are some of the largest turbines at this unpermitted facility and have the greatest potential for pollution.

The company’s failure to get a permit for its power plant — which is located near homes, schools, and churches — creates added health risks for families in North Mississippi and Memphis. It’s also a clear violation of the Clean Air Act, which requires major sources of pollution to obtain air permits, which include stringent pollution limits and require the use of pollution controls, before being constructed or operated.

“The urgency of ensuring that our communities’ health and environment are protected is clear,” said Abre’ Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice. “By expanding an unpermitted power plant despite decades of clear direction for permitting, xAI is showing a blatant disregard for the law. xAI was already violating the law then showed no remorse by adding six more turbines that further exacerbates the health risks facing families in North Mississippi and the Greater Memphis region. We will not stand by and idly watch as the Clean Air Act is ignored. We will continue to fight to ensure all polluters, including billionaires’ companies, understand that the law is not to be treated as a suggestion while local communities bear the consequences.”

Toxic emissions from the facility threaten to do long-lasting harm to nearby communities. Pollution from gas turbines includes smog-forming nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter, and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde. These pollutants are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers.

“We put these companies on notice that their toxic air pollution is both dangerous and illegal. Rather than stop, they’ve added more turbines capable of inflicting even more harm to the surrounding communities,” says Laura Thoms, the director of enforcement for Earthjustice . “We’re asking the judge to halt all unpermitted pollution and make sure xAI follows the law to protect people put at risk by their illegal operations.”

“We’ve warned xAI for months that its operation of unpermitted gas turbines violates federal law. But instead of fixing these issues, xAI installed six more massive turbines to its personal power plant, increasing the amount of illegal pollution that it can pump into nearby communities,” Ben Grillot, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center , said. “We’re asking the court to force xAI to immediately stop the use of these turbines in order to protect communities in North Mississippi and Memphis from the tech company’s harmful pollution.”

In January, the Environmental Protection Agency confirmed that large methane gas turbines — like the ones used at xAI’s power plant—require construction and air permits.

A federal judge in Mississippi has rejected an effort by the Trump administration to shut down a lawsuit brought by the NAACP against Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, allowing a closely watched environmental justice case to continue. The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act. The plant supplies power to xAI’s massive Colossus 2 data center, which supports the company’s artificial intelligence operations. The case has drawn attention because of the plant’s location near predominantly Black communities in North Mississippi and South Memphis. Reuters previously reported that pollution tied to the project has raised concerns about whether the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is placing disproportionate environmental burdens on Black neighborhoods. The Trump administration, acting through the Environmental Protection Agency, sought to intervene in the case and argued that the EPA had the authority to terminate the lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown disagreed with that position Monday. Brown ruled that the EPA could participate in the case, but said nothing in the Clean Air Act gives the agency the power to unilaterally dismiss a citizen lawsuit simply because it has intervened. The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved. The lawsuit was originally filed in April. At the time, the NAACP accused xAI of operating dozens of methane gas turbines without the required permits, effectively creating a private power plant to meet the enormous energy demands of its data center. The organization has argued that nearby residents should not have to bear the health and environmental costs of the company’s rapid expansion. The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution. The organization is being represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice. The legal fight comes as communities across the country begin confronting the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, and developers are increasingly turning to on-site power generation to meet demand. That growth has prompted new questions about air quality, energy use and how quickly environmental regulations can keep pace with the AI boom. For the NAACP, the case is about more than one data center. It is part of a broader argument that Black communities should not be expected to absorb additional pollution in the name of technological progress, particularly when those communities have historically faced disproportionate exposure to industrial development and poor air quality. The judge’s ruling does not determine whether xAI violated environmental law. That question still has to be resolved in court. What it does mean is that the NAACP will be allowed to continue pressing its case.

The judge's decision to let the case proceed past preliminary motions means xAI will now face discovery and potentially a trial on the merits of the NAACP's claims. Just last week, SpaceX closed a massive $40 billion debt deal to purchase GPUs for AI infrastructure, underscoring the breakneck pace of expansion across Musk's technology empire. That infrastructure buildout requires enormous data centers with corresponding energy demands and environmental footprints. The NAACP's lawsuit centers on allegations that xAI's data center operations produce air pollution that exceeds Clean Air Act thresholds without proper permitting or mitigation measures. Environmental advocates have increasingly raised concerns about the energy intensity of AI model training and inference, which requires thousands of high-powered chips running continuously in facilities that generate substantial heat and emissions. Data centers have become flashpoints in communities across the country as residents push back against facilities they see as bringing pollution, noise, and strain on local power grids without commensurate benefits. The judge's ruling doesn't determine the merits of the NAACP's claims, but it does mean the organization cleared the initial hurdles to proceed with litigation. That's significant because tech companies often succeed in getting environmental lawsuits dismissed on procedural grounds before reaching the substance of the allegations. For xAI, the lawsuit adds regulatory uncertainty at a crucial moment. The company competes with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in the race to build more powerful AI systems, a competition that requires massive infrastructure investments. Companies have announced plans for dozens of new data centers to support AI workloads, often in regions offering tax incentives or cheap power. Legal experts say the case could establish important precedents about what level of environmental review and permitting AI data centers require. The Clean Air Act includes provisions for reviewing major new sources of pollution and protecting communities disproportionately affected by environmental hazards, both potentially relevant to large-scale AI infrastructure. The lawsuit also highlights tensions within Musk's broader business empire. The company's rapid growth has occasionally outpaced its ability to navigate complex regulatory frameworks. The case now moves into discovery, where the NAACP will have the opportunity to gather evidence about xAI's operations, emissions, and compliance with air quality standards. That process could reveal new details about how the company manages the environmental impacts of its data center operations and whether it obtained necessary permits before beginning operations. For the NAACP, the ruling represents validation of its strategy to use environmental law as a tool for protecting communities from the potential harms of AI infrastructure expansion. The organization has increasingly focused on technology policy issues, recognizing that decisions about where to locate data centers and other facilities have significant equity implications. The judge's decision to let this lawsuit proceed signals that AI companies can't assume their infrastructure expansion will face only technical and financial hurdles. As xAI and its rivals pour billions into data centers, they'll need to navigate not just the engineering challenges of training massive models, but also the regulatory and legal frameworks designed to protect air quality and environmental justice.

This request follows the organization’s Clean Air Act enforcement lawsuit filed last month . The NAACP is represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice in the case. In February, the NAACP notified xAI and its subsidiary that their personal power plant consisting of 27 gas-fired turbines violated the Clean Air Act and put the health of local communities at risk. These six new turbines — which on their own would be considered a major source of pollution under the Clean Air Act — are some of the largest turbines at this unpermitted facility and have the greatest potential for pollution. The company’s failure to get a permit for its power plant — which is located near homes, schools, and churches — creates added health risks for families in North Mississippi and Memphis. It’s also a clear violation of the Clean Air Act, which requires major sources of pollution to obtain air permits, which include stringent pollution limits and require the use of pollution controls, before being constructed or operated. “The urgency of ensuring that our communities’ health and environment are protected is clear,” said Abre’ Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice. “By expanding an unpermitted power plant despite decades of clear direction for permitting, xAI is showing a blatant disregard for the law. xAI was already violating the law then showed no remorse by adding six more turbines that further exacerbates the health risks facing families in North Mississippi and the Greater Memphis region.
