Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s. At the same time, Wall Street investors have been bidding up the price of some complicated financial instruments that insure corporate debt against default, like those insuring SoftBank, the Japanese technology colossus that has borrowed heavily to bet its future on a partnership with OpenAI. The recent market moves could spell losses for investors that own the companies’ existing bonds and could mean the companies will be forced to pay higher interest rates when they borrow again, raising the costs of their already wildly expensive AI projects. facts.text: Quarterly earnings reports from hyperscalers this week spooked investors.
Alphabet saw its cash flow sink deeper into negative territory in the third quarter, with the Google parent also joining Meta and Amazon in charging ahead with massive spending plans.
On Thursday, Alphabet fell about 12%, its worst day on record.
The funding round was also upstaged by Anthropic, according to the report, as OpenAI's arch-rival prepares to go public next month.
Meanwhile, S&P sees Meta's capex reaching $140 billion this year, topping $225 billion in 2027, hitting $252 billion in 2028, and then flattening out from there.
At the same time, OpenAI was seeking more capital just as other AI giants tapped financial markets heavily.
This past week alone, Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in a bond sale.
Following a brutal selloff in tech stocks over the past week, OpenAI slashed the target on its latest fundraising round to $20 billion from $30 billion, sources told the Financial Times .
That also cut its expected valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion.

The prospect of hyperscalers continuing to hemorrhage funds was too much for S&P Global, which cut its outlook on Meta to "negative" from "stable" late Friday, citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around capital expenditure ​plans.
The credit ratings agency maintained Meta at AA- but warned ⁠the social media leader's leverage could top 1.0x as soon as 2027, which is the downgrade threshold for the current rating.
That's up from about 0.1x in 2025 and primarily reflects its strategy of leasing data center capacity rather than from its debt issuance.

The bearish environment on Wall Street also comes as rising bond yields have sent borrowing costs sharply higher, the political backlash against data centers is expected to help Democrats retake Congress, and the Iran war could re-escalate after midterm elections.

"We believe the technology and infrastructure we're building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone."

In a statement to Fortune , a Meta spokesperson said the company disagrees with S&P's assessment of its AI monetization capabilities, pointing to "significant product and business opportunities" ahead.
Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have outlined more than $740 billion in capital spending this year, exposing cracks emerging spending boom as investors question the cost of AI infrastructure.
The spending boom is also being financed through borrowing and securities sales, not only through profits.
For investors, that question now sits alongside the companies’ latest cash-flow figures and spending plans.
The broader question is whether companies facing debt trouble like CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank are the industry’s weak links or are harbingers of deeper problems in the AI build-out.
Investors have sold off bonds for other AI giants as well, including Larry Ellison’s company, Oracle, though the price declines are not as steep as CoreWeave’s.
Not every data centre developer worries bond investors equally.
The larger so-called hyperscalers, such as Meta and Alphabet, which continue to borrow heavily, have been forced by investors to pay only modestly more in interest in recent debt deals.
The cost of insuring against losses on SoftBank’s debt has spiked.
It now costs more than US$40,000 to insure against US$1 million of SoftBank debt.
At the beginning of 2026, the cost was less than US$27,000.
Those questions burst into the forefront this past week when investors rapidly lost confidence in one debt-laden data centre company, CoreWeave.

Prices of its bonds – the company has accrued US$72 billion in liabilities to operate 51 data centres – crashed, and investors placed a more than 60 per cent likelihood that CoreWeave would fail to meet its obligations.
Oracle has faced slowdowns on multiple projects.
SoftBank has borrowed heavily to make one of the biggest bets – by dollar value – on OpenAI.
The Japanese conglomerate, led by Masayoshi Son, wrote its first US$500 million check in 2024 and a year later invested US$30 billion more.
That is just a year before Oracle’s debt comes due.
Some of the debt has traded around US$0.90 on the US dollar or below that, according to two traders, a steep drop for a relatively new loan.
CoreWeave’s business model defies easy description.
Its financial arrangements have been compared by some investors and analysts with those of the troubled office-space provider WeWork.
Oracle planned to pay back the borrowed money on the Texas facility helped by profits from the latter complex, called Project Lighthouse, which it expected to be operational by 2028.
In response to questions about SoftBank’s increasing debt, Alex Clavel, CEO of the SoftBank Vision Funds, said the amount of debt as a percentage of SoftBank Group’s assets had not changed.

contextFacts.text: "Meta is already delivering stronger engagement, better recommendations, and greater returns for businesses as a result of AI investments," the spokesperson continued.

"We believe the technology and infrastructure we're building now will open new revenue streams, create long-term shareholder value, and bring us closer to delivering personal superintelligence to everyone."
Meta's rivals, however, are monetizing their data centers by leasing compute capacity, including to frontier model labs and enterprise customers, it added.
OpenAI didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The English-language global edition of JournalArta.
TRILLIONS of dollars in borrowed money have powered the artificial intelligence boom.
First, CoreWeave buys Nvidia and other AI chips.
Then, as with WeWork, which leases space inside office buildings owned by others, CoreWeave contracts with data centre owners to use the structures for AI computing for 15 years or more.
CoreWeave then sub-leases the space to customers, including Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI, for a shorter time frame.
Several investors said they worried about whether hyperscalers like Meta and Microsoft would even need to lease space from CoreWeave in the future.
Alternately, they are wary of whether the data centres could become dated or even obsolete as their existing contracts expire.
Oracle faces similar permitting issues at a data centre project in New Mexico.
The project’s developer, investment firm Blue Owl, has started construction on the facility, but Oracle is struggling to get state permits to provide enough power.

The rub is that CoreWeave is on the hook for costs on both ends: It must pay to assemble and operate the facilities before any tenant is in place, and it is committed to the space for longer than its customers may stick around.

The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday. The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5bn Bybit hack last year. The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum . The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.” On Thursday, $6.3bn in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack. The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed. The hackers were able to manipulate a system used to approve transactions to move money out of a Binance-controlled, internet-connected so-called "hot" wallet in a way that did not pass through normal approval controls, Teng said. "Rest assured that ​we are working nonstop to resolve this, to make the users whole, and live up to your trust," Teng wrote. Binance's BNB token was down about 6.4% over the past 24 hours at $696. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. "This incident is almost certainly the single-largest-known theft of any kind," British blockchain analysts Elliptic said. A federal judge in Mississippi has rejected an effort by the Trump administration to shut down a lawsuit brought by the NAACP against Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, allowing a closely watched environmental justice case to continue. The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act. The plant supplies power to xAI’s massive Colossus 2 data center, which supports the company’s artificial intelligence operations. The case has drawn attention because of the plant’s location near predominantly Black communities in North Mississippi and South Memphis. Reuters previously reported that pollution tied to the project has raised concerns about whether the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is placing disproportionate environmental burdens on Black neighborhoods. The Trump administration, acting through the Environmental Protection Agency, sought to intervene in the case and argued that the EPA had the authority to terminate the lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown disagreed with that position Monday. Brown ruled that the EPA could participate in the case, but said nothing in the Clean Air Act gives the agency the power to unilaterally dismiss a citizen lawsuit simply because it has intervened. The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved. The lawsuit was originally filed in April. At the time, the NAACP accused xAI of operating dozens of methane gas turbines without the required permits, effectively creating a private power plant to meet the enormous energy demands of its data center. The organization has argued that nearby residents should not have to bear the health and environmental costs of the company’s rapid expansion. The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution. The organization is being represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice. The legal fight comes as communities across the country begin confronting the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, and developers are increasingly turning to on-site power generation to meet demand. That growth has prompted new questions about air quality, energy use and how quickly environmental regulations can keep pace with the AI boom. For the NAACP, the case is about more than one data center. It is part of a broader argument that Black communities should not be expected to absorb additional pollution in the name of technological progress, particularly when those communities have historically faced disproportionate exposure to industrial development and poor air quality. The judge’s ruling does not determine whether xAI violated environmental law. That question still has to be resolved in court. What it does mean is that the NAACP will be allowed to continue pressing its case.

extraction.body: A federal judge just handed the NAACP a major victory in its fight against xAI, allowing a lawsuit alleging Clean Air Act violations at the company's data center to move forward. With AI data centers consuming unprecedented amounts of energy and requiring extensive cooling systems, the ruling could reshape how tech companies approach regulatory compliance. The legal battle puts xAI, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence venture, squarely in the crosshairs of environmental justice advocates who argue the company's data center operations violate federal clean air standards. The judge's decision to let the case proceed past preliminary motions means xAI will now face discovery and potentially a trial on the merits of the NAACP's claims. Just last week, SpaceX closed a massive $40 billion debt deal to purchase GPUs for AI infrastructure, underscoring the breakneck pace of expansion across Musk's technology empire. That infrastructure buildout requires enormous data centers with corresponding energy demands and environmental footprints. The NAACP's lawsuit centers on allegations that xAI's data center operations produce air pollution that exceeds Clean Air Act thresholds without proper permitting or mitigation measures. Environmental advocates have increasingly raised concerns about the energy intensity of AI model training and inference, which requires thousands of high-powered chips running continuously in facilities that generate substantial heat and emissions. Data centers have become flashpoints in communities across the country as residents push back against facilities they see as bringing pollution, noise, and strain on local power grids without commensurate benefits. The judge's ruling doesn't determine the merits of the NAACP's claims, but it does mean the organization cleared the initial hurdles to proceed with litigation. That's significant because tech companies often succeed in getting environmental lawsuits dismissed on procedural grounds before reaching the substance of the allegations. For xAI, the lawsuit adds regulatory uncertainty at a crucial moment. The company competes with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in the race to build more powerful AI systems, a competition that requires massive infrastructure investments. Companies have announced plans for dozens of new data centers to support AI workloads, often in regions offering tax incentives or cheap power. Legal experts say the case could establish important precedents about what level of environmental review and permitting AI data centers require. The Clean Air Act includes provisions for reviewing major new sources of pollution and protecting communities disproportionately affected by environmental hazards, both potentially relevant to large-scale AI infrastructure. The lawsuit also highlights tensions within Musk's broader business empire. The company's rapid growth has occasionally outpaced its ability to navigate complex regulatory frameworks. The case now moves into discovery, where the NAACP will have the opportunity to gather evidence about xAI's operations, emissions, and compliance with air quality standards. That process could reveal new details about how the company manages the environmental impacts of its data center operations and whether it obtained necessary permits before beginning operations. For the NAACP, the ruling represents validation of its strategy to use environmental law as a tool for protecting communities from the potential harms of AI infrastructure expansion. The organization has increasingly focused on technology policy issues, recognizing that decisions about where to locate data centers and other facilities have significant equity implications. The judge's decision to let this lawsuit proceed signals that AI companies can't assume their infrastructure expansion will face only technical and financial hurdles. As xAI and its rivals pour billions into data centers, they'll need to navigate not just the engineering challenges of training massive models, but also the regulatory and legal frameworks designed to protect air quality and environmental justice.

In February, the NAACP notified xAI and its subsidiary that their personal power plant consisting of 27 gas-fired turbines violated the Clean Air Act and put the health of local communities at risk. These six new turbines — which on their own would be considered a major source of pollution under the Clean Air Act — are some of the largest turbines at this unpermitted facility and have the greatest potential for pollution. The company’s failure to get a permit for its power plant — which is located near homes, schools, and churches — creates added health risks for families in North Mississippi and Memphis. Today, the NAACP filed a request for a preliminary injunction to stop unpermitted air pollution from an illegal power plant built by Elon Musk’s company, xAI, and its subsidiary, MZX Tech. The unpermitted power plant, which is located in Southaven, Mississippi, powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data center in Memphis.
This request follows the organization’s Clean Air Act enforcement lawsuit filed last month . The NAACP is represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice in the case.

In February, the NAACP notified xAI and its subsidiary that their personal power plant consisting of 27 gas-fired turbines violated the Clean Air Act and put the health of local communities at risk. But instead of fixing these problems and complying with federal law, the tech companies did the opposite: they brought six additional gas turbines on site, bringing the total number of turbines at the power plant to 33. These six new turbines — which on their own would be considered a major source of pollution under the Clean Air Act — are some of the largest turbines at this unpermitted facility and have the greatest potential for pollution.

The company’s failure to get a permit for its power plant — which is located near homes, schools, and churches — creates added health risks for families in North Mississippi and Memphis. It’s also a clear violation of the Clean Air Act, which requires major sources of pollution to obtain air permits, which include stringent pollution limits and require the use of pollution controls, before being constructed or operated.

“The urgency of ensuring that our communities’ health and environment are protected is clear,” said Abre’ Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice. “By expanding an unpermitted power plant despite decades of clear direction for permitting, xAI is showing a blatant disregard for the law. xAI was already violating the law then showed no remorse by adding six more turbines that further exacerbates the health risks facing families in North Mississippi and the Greater Memphis region. We will not stand by and idly watch as the Clean Air Act is ignored. We will continue to fight to ensure all polluters, including billionaires’ companies, understand that the law is not to be treated as a suggestion while local communities bear the consequences.”

Toxic emissions from the facility threaten to do long-lasting harm to nearby communities. Pollution from gas turbines includes smog-forming nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter, and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde. These pollutants are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers.

“We put these companies on notice that their toxic air pollution is both dangerous and illegal. Rather than stop, they’ve added more turbines capable of inflicting even more harm to the surrounding communities,” says Laura Thoms, the director of enforcement for Earthjustice . “We’re asking the judge to halt all unpermitted pollution and make sure xAI follows the law to protect people put at risk by their illegal operations.”

“We’ve warned xAI for months that its operation of unpermitted gas turbines violates federal law. But instead of fixing these issues, xAI installed six more massive turbines to its personal power plant, increasing the amount of illegal pollution that it can pump into nearby communities,” Ben Grillot, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center , said. “We’re asking the court to force xAI to immediately stop the use of these turbines in order to protect communities in North Mississippi and Memphis from the tech company’s harmful pollution.”

In January, the Environmental Protection Agency confirmed that large methane gas turbines — like the ones used at xAI’s power plant—require construction and air permits.

coreStoryFacts.text: A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis.

Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act.
“Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.”

In a statement , the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month )

Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.”

The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved.

The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act.
The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution.

The unpermitted power plant, which is located in Southaven, Mississippi, powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data center in Memphis.

But instead of fixing these issues, xAI installed six more massive turbines to its personal power plant, increasing the amount of illegal pollution that it can pump into nearby communities,” Ben Grillot, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center , said.
“We’re asking the court to force xAI to immediately stop the use of these turbines in order to protect communities in North Mississippi and Memphis from the tech company’s harmful pollution.”
“We put these companies on notice that their toxic air pollution is both dangerous and illegal.

This request follows the organization’s Clean Air Act enforcement lawsuit filed last month .

A federal judge in Mississippi has rejected an effort by the Trump administration to shut down a lawsuit brought by the NAACP against Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, allowing a closely watched environmental justice case to continue. The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act. The plant supplies power to xAI’s massive Colossus 2 data center, which supports the company’s artificial intelligence operations. The case has drawn attention because of the plant’s location near predominantly Black communities in North Mississippi and South Memphis. Reuters previously reported that pollution tied to the project has raised concerns about whether the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure is placing disproportionate environmental burdens on Black neighborhoods. The Trump administration, acting through the Environmental Protection Agency, sought to intervene in the case and argued that the EPA had the authority to terminate the lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Debra Brown disagreed with that position Monday. Brown ruled that the EPA could participate in the case, but said nothing in the Clean Air Act gives the agency the power to unilaterally dismiss a citizen lawsuit simply because it has intervened. The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved. The lawsuit was originally filed in April. At the time, the NAACP accused xAI of operating dozens of methane gas turbines without the required permits, effectively creating a private power plant to meet the enormous energy demands of its data center. The organization has argued that nearby residents should not have to bear the health and environmental costs of the company’s rapid expansion. The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution. The organization is being represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice. The legal fight comes as communities across the country begin confronting the environmental footprint of artificial intelligence. Data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, and developers are increasingly turning to on-site power generation to meet demand. That growth has prompted new questions about air quality, energy use and how quickly environmental regulations can keep pace with the AI boom. For the NAACP, the case is about more than one data center. It is part of a broader argument that Black communities should not be expected to absorb additional pollution in the name of technological progress, particularly when those communities have historically faced disproportionate exposure to industrial development and poor air quality. The judge’s ruling does not determine whether xAI violated environmental law. That question still has to be resolved in court. What it does mean is that the NAACP will be allowed to continue pressing its case.

extraction.body: A federal judge just handed the NAACP a major victory in its fight against xAI, allowing a lawsuit alleging Clean Air Act violations at the company's data center to move forward. With AI data centers consuming unprecedented amounts of energy and requiring extensive cooling systems, the ruling could reshape how tech companies approach regulatory compliance. The legal battle puts xAI, Elon Musk's artificial intelligence venture, squarely in the crosshairs of environmental justice advocates who argue the company's data center operations violate federal clean air standards. The judge's decision to let the case proceed past preliminary motions means xAI will now face discovery and potentially a trial on the merits of the NAACP's claims. Just last week, SpaceX closed a massive $40 billion debt deal to purchase GPUs for AI infrastructure, underscoring the breakneck pace of expansion across Musk's technology empire. That infrastructure buildout requires enormous data centers with corresponding energy demands and environmental footprints. The NAACP's lawsuit centers on allegations that xAI's data center operations produce air pollution that exceeds Clean Air Act thresholds without proper permitting or mitigation measures. Environmental advocates have increasingly raised concerns about the energy intensity of AI model training and inference, which requires thousands of high-powered chips running continuously in facilities that generate substantial heat and emissions. Data centers have become flashpoints in communities across the country as residents push back against facilities they see as bringing pollution, noise, and strain on local power grids without commensurate benefits. The judge's ruling doesn't determine the merits of the NAACP's claims, but it does mean the organization cleared the initial hurdles to proceed with litigation. That's significant because tech companies often succeed in getting environmental lawsuits dismissed on procedural grounds before reaching the substance of the allegations. For xAI, the lawsuit adds regulatory uncertainty at a crucial moment. The company competes with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Meta in the race to build more powerful AI systems, a competition that requires massive infrastructure investments. Companies have announced plans for dozens of new data centers to support AI workloads, often in regions offering tax incentives or cheap power. Legal experts say the case could establish important precedents about what level of environmental review and permitting AI data centers require. The Clean Air Act includes provisions for reviewing major new sources of pollution and protecting communities disproportionately affected by environmental hazards, both potentially relevant to large-scale AI infrastructure. The lawsuit also highlights tensions within Musk's broader business empire. The company's rapid growth has occasionally outpaced its ability to navigate complex regulatory frameworks. The case now moves into discovery, where the NAACP will have the opportunity to gather evidence about xAI's operations, emissions, and compliance with air quality standards. That process could reveal new details about how the company manages the environmental impacts of its data center operations and whether it obtained necessary permits before beginning operations. For the NAACP, the ruling represents validation of its strategy to use environmental law as a tool for protecting communities from the potential harms of AI infrastructure expansion. The organization has increasingly focused on technology policy issues, recognizing that decisions about where to locate data centers and other facilities have significant equity implications. The judge's decision to let this lawsuit proceed signals that AI companies can't assume their infrastructure expansion will face only technical and financial hurdles. As xAI and its rivals pour billions into data centers, they'll need to navigate not just the engineering challenges of training massive models, but also the regulatory and legal frameworks designed to protect air quality and environmental justice.

Instead of addressing its Clean Air Act violations, Elon Musk’s company added even more unpermitted gas turbines to its illegal powerplant — saddling nearby communities with harmful toxic emissions Alexandria Trimble, atrimble@earthjustice.org Today, the NAACP filed a request for a preliminary injunction to stop unpermitted air pollution from an illegal power plant built by Elon Musk’s company, xAI, and its subsidiary, MZX Tech. The unpermitted power plant, which is located in Southaven, Mississippi, powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data center in Memphis. This request follows the organization’s Clean Air Act enforcement lawsuit filed last month . The NAACP is represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice in the case. In February, the NAACP notified xAI and its subsidiary that their personal power plant consisting of 27 gas-fired turbines violated the Clean Air Act and put the health of local communities at risk. But instead of fixing these problems and complying with federal law, the tech companies did the opposite: they brought six additional gas turbines on site, bringing the total number of turbines at the power plant to 33. These six new turbines — which on their own would be considered a major source of pollution under the Clean Air Act — are some of the largest turbines at this unpermitted facility and have the greatest potential for pollution. The company’s failure to get a permit for its power plant — which is located near homes, schools, and churches — creates added health risks for families in North Mississippi and Memphis. It’s also a clear violation of the Clean Air Act, which requires major sources of pollution to obtain air permits, which include stringent pollution limits and require the use of pollution controls, before being constructed or operated. “The urgency of ensuring that our communities’ health and environment are protected is clear,” said Abre’ Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice. “By expanding an unpermitted power plant despite decades of clear direction for permitting, xAI is showing a blatant disregard for the law. xAI was already violating the law then showed no remorse by adding six more turbines that further exacerbates the health risks facing families in North Mississippi and the Greater Memphis region. We will not stand by and idly watch as the Clean Air Act is ignored. We will continue to fight to ensure all polluters, including billionaires’ companies, understand that the law is not to be treated as a suggestion while local communities bear the consequences.” Toxic emissions from the facility threaten to do long-lasting harm to nearby communities. Pollution from gas turbines includes smog-forming nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter, and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde. These pollutants are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers. “We put these companies on notice that their toxic air pollution is both dangerous and illegal. Rather than stop, they’ve added more turbines capable of inflicting even more harm to the surrounding communities,” says Laura Thoms, the director of enforcement for Earthjustice . “We’re asking the judge to halt all unpermitted pollution and make sure xAI follows the law to protect people put at risk by their illegal operations.” “We’ve warned xAI for months that its operation of unpermitted gas turbines violates federal law. But instead of fixing these issues, xAI installed six more massive turbines to its personal power plant, increasing the amount of illegal pollution that it can pump into nearby communities,” Ben Grillot, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center , said. “We’re asking the court to force xAI to immediately stop the use of these turbines in order to protect communities in North Mississippi and Memphis from the tech company’s harmful pollution.” The 33 unpermitted gas turbines that make up xAI’s power plant have the potential to emit a staggering amount of toxic air pollution each year: Data for blue bars (permitted facilities): EPA, 2020 National Emissions Inventory Data ; Ex. A-25 (PSD Air Permit for MZX fleet); Ex. A-2 (Shelby County’s Colossus 1 Permit for CTC fleet); Ex. H (Laufenberg Decl.) ¶ 31. Case: 3:26-cv-00074-MPM-JMV Doc #20. In January, the Environmental Protection Agency confirmed that large methane gas turbines — like the ones used at xAI’s power plant—require construction and air permits. NAACP’s request for a preliminary injunction asks the court to take emergency action to immediately halt xAI’s illegal and dangerous pollution in order to protect nearby communities that are facing imminent health harms. Instead of addressing its Clean Air Act violations, Elon Musk’s company added even more unpermitted gas turbines to its illegal powerplant — saddling nearby communities with harmful toxic emissions
Alexandria Trimble, atrimble@earthjustice.org

Today, the NAACP filed a request for a preliminary injunction to stop unpermitted air pollution from an illegal power plant built by Elon Musk’s company, xAI, and its subsidiary, MZX Tech. The unpermitted power plant, which is located in Southaven, Mississippi, powers xAI’s Colossus 2 data center in Memphis.
This request follows the organization’s Clean Air Act enforcement lawsuit filed last month . The NAACP is represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice in the case.

In February, the NAACP notified xAI and its subsidiary that their personal power plant consisting of 27 gas-fired turbines violated the Clean Air Act and put the health of local communities at risk. But instead of fixing these problems and complying with federal law, the tech companies did the opposite: they brought six additional gas turbines on site, bringing the total number of turbines at the power plant to 33. These six new turbines — which on their own would be considered a major source of pollution under the Clean Air Act — are some of the largest turbines at this unpermitted facility and have the greatest potential for pollution.

The company’s failure to get a permit for its power plant — which is located near homes, schools, and churches — creates added health risks for families in North Mississippi and Memphis. It’s also a clear violation of the Clean Air Act, which requires major sources of pollution to obtain air permits, which include stringent pollution limits and require the use of pollution controls, before being constructed or operated.

“The urgency of ensuring that our communities’ health and environment are protected is clear,” said Abre’ Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice. “By expanding an unpermitted power plant despite decades of clear direction for permitting, xAI is showing a blatant disregard for the law. xAI was already violating the law then showed no remorse by adding six more turbines that further exacerbates the health risks facing families in North Mississippi and the Greater Memphis region. We will not stand by and idly watch as the Clean Air Act is ignored. We will continue to fight to ensure all polluters, including billionaires’ companies, understand that the law is not to be treated as a suggestion while local communities bear the consequences.”

Toxic emissions from the facility threaten to do long-lasting harm to nearby communities. Pollution from gas turbines includes smog-forming nitrogen oxides, fine particulate matter, and hazardous chemicals like formaldehyde. These pollutants are tied to increases in asthma, respiratory diseases, heart problems, and certain cancers.

“We put these companies on notice that their toxic air pollution is both dangerous and illegal. Rather than stop, they’ve added more turbines capable of inflicting even more harm to the surrounding communities,” says Laura Thoms, the director of enforcement for Earthjustice . “We’re asking the judge to halt all unpermitted pollution and make sure xAI follows the law to protect people put at risk by their illegal operations.”

“We’ve warned xAI for months that its operation of unpermitted gas turbines violates federal law. But instead of fixing these issues, xAI installed six more massive turbines to its personal power plant, increasing the amount of illegal pollution that it can pump into nearby communities,” Ben Grillot, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center , said. “We’re asking the court to force xAI to immediately stop the use of these turbines in order to protect communities in North Mississippi and Memphis from the tech company’s harmful pollution.”

In January, the Environmental Protection Agency confirmed that large methane gas turbines — like the ones used at xAI’s power plant—require construction and air permits.

NAACP’s request for a preliminary injunction asks the court to take emergency action to immediately halt xAI’s illegal and dangerous pollution in order to protect nearby communities that are facing imminent health harms.

story.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward

facts.text: A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis.

Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act.
“Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.”

In a statement , the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month )

Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.”

A federal judge in Mississippi has rejected an effort by the Trump administration to shut down a lawsuit brought by the NAACP against Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, xAI, allowing a closely watched environmental justice case to continue.
The ruling keeps the NAACP’s challenge alive while allowing the federal government to remain involved.

The lawsuit, filed by the national NAACP and its Mississippi State Conference, accuses xAI and its subsidiary, MZX Tech, of operating a gas-fired power plant in Southaven, Mississippi, without the environmental permits required under the Clean Air Act.
The NAACP later asked the court for emergency action to stop what it described as ongoing unpermitted pollution.
A federal judge just handed the NAACP a major victory in its fight against xAI, allowing a lawsuit alleging Clean Air Act violations at the company's data center to move forward.

Data centers have become flashpoints in communities across the country as residents push back against facilities they see as bringing pollution, noise, and strain on local power grids without commensurate benefits.
The judge's decision to let the case proceed past preliminary motions means xAI will now face discovery and potentially a trial on the merits of the NAACP's claims.

passages: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update .

Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.
The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.
The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights.
"The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said.

Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable.
"A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC.
A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC.
TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.
Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly.
He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets.
The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

extraction.body: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update . The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks. Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000. Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. "A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC. Redbord said law enforcement typically obtains a court order or seizure warrant before working with stablecoin issuers to release or reissue assets and return them to their rightful owners. "Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract," he said. "Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim." But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers. "There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC. Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance. The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach. Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors. "The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said. Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds. Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets. "I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly," Farrell said. The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton. Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable. "We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals," Perkins said. Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model. He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders. Got a confidential news tip? extraction.body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has reportedly suffered a major cyberattack, with hackers stealing cryptocurrencies worth $6.3 billion in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history. Confirming the incident, Binance said it was working to contain and resolve what it described as a "complex attack". The exchange said it was coordinating with law enforcement agencies and other industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen assets. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance wrote in a post on X. The exchange also cautioned that the estimated value of the stolen assets could rise further as investigations continue. The $6.3-billion figure may "continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," it said. Here's what we know about the reported Binance hack so far. What Happened? $6.3 Billion In Cryptocurrency Stolen According to Binance, around $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies were stolen from wallets used by the exchange to process transactions. In its initial assessment, the company believed the attack had originated from a compromised laptop. However, further investigation revealed additional security breaches. "However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance said. The attack targeted Binance.com, the exchange's global centralised platform. Binance.US, which serves customers in the United States, was not affected, the company said. Binance said the compromised laptop provided the attacker with access to a service container, enabling the submission of unauthorised withdrawal transactions. Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, described the incident as a "complex attack process". According to US-based blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance's "signing infrastructure", which authorises transactions. This allegedly allowed them to issue instructions that drained the affected wallets. ALSO READ: Mohan Yadav Announces 2% DA Hike From January 2026 For MP Govt Employees Blockchain records indicate that the bulk of the heist took place within approximately 20 minutes. After moving the funds, the attackers attempted to transfer them beyond the reach of Binance's counterparties and stablecoin issuers. These entities have since frozen roughly half of the stolen assets. Binance and other authorities have not confirmed the identity of those responsible for the attack. However, US-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs has attributed the hack to a North Korean-linked group known as TraderTraitor, which it described as one of North Korea's elite hacking units. In a post on its website on Thursday, TRM said: "We make this judgment with high confidence." Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis also pointed towards the same group. Its co-founder and CEO, Jonathan Levin, wrote on X that the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK (North Korea) group TraderTraitor". Binance said on Friday that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to manage the fallout from the attack. This includes $5 billion already held in the affected token assets. In an earlier statement, Teng said users' funds were safe. As a precautionary measure, the exchange also temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals. The company said it was working with its partners to freeze assets worth $3 billion that have been traced so far. However, freezing the assets does not necessarily mean they will be returned to Binance. It does, nevertheless, restrict the hackers' ability to convert the stolen cryptocurrencies into cash. Binance also said it remained on schedule to restore withdrawal services. "We are still on track towards the expected timeline to resume the withdrawal service in 45 hours," the exchange said. ALSO READ: Money Matters: Why Financial Conversations Remain Taboo In Indian Households

passages: Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation.
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.
Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X.
Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said.
Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: "We're looking at that."
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists."

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."
In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked.
The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
"Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines."
"We are working nonstop to resolve this," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X.
Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet.
"User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said.
"The vast majority sits in cold wallets" — which are offline and used for secure storage — "and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal."
Left: Binance logo and hacker code are seen in this illustration taken Oct.
Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.

Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

extraction.body: Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit. The company said it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets and was beginning to recover assets for users. Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. WATCH: $6 billion cryptocurrency heist puts investors on edge The cryptocurrency exchange has promised to cover all losses, and it has been sharing regular updates on its social media channels as it uncovers more information about the hack. "We are working nonstop to resolve this," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X. In an exchange Friday with reporters at the White House, President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were investigating the Binance hack. Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: "We're looking at that." Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation. Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach." U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM, in a post on its website late Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said. "An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists." Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice." Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties. In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the world's best. While about half of the stolen assets were frozen, there is evidence that the hackers already are transferring and converting some of what wasn't recovered, said Garrick Hileman, an independent cryptocurrency analyst. "Like in money laundering, you bring in the stolen goods and launder those through a mixer or tumbler," he said. "You mix it in with other cryptos, and it's harder to track." TRM and several other crypto firms and experts have said the hack represents the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack. TRM listed the Bybit hack when it referenced similarities between the Binance hack and previous attacks linked to TraderTraitor. Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, wrote on X that while Binance's hack might be the largest in terms of its dollar value, previous attacks on other companies like the crypto exchange Mt. Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said. Experts warn this scale of hacking could become more commonplace. "A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI," said Andy Ward, a senior vice president at Absolute Security. "Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines." The hack has raised questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, co-founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab. "This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet. Teng, Binance's co-CEO, confirmed in a nearly five-minute video posted on X Friday that Binance's own hot wallet was affected. "User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said. "The vast majority sits in cold wallets" — which are offline and used for secure storage — "and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal." Teng said Binance's tech and security teams are "still deep" in investigating the hack. He said it was not carried out by one person and that the attackers used complex tactics, including a "self-destruct mechanism" that is making the incident more difficult to investigate. "We are working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other exchanges to trace and recover stolen funds," Teng said. "We will do everything within our power to make sure that these bad actors will be held accountable." Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. Associated Press journalists John Seewer, Aamer Madhani, Hyung-jin Kim and Kim Tong-hyung contributed to this report. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update . The exchange pledged to cover all losses, while blockchain investigators linked the attack to North Korea and analysts assessed the potential financial risks. Bitcoin was under pressure on Friday and was trading below $78,000. Freezing cryptocurrency prevents it from being transferred, but recovering the funds requires a separate legal process, according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs and a former U.S. federal prosecutor and Treasury official. "Stablecoins are the most recoverable asset class in crypto because the issuer controls the token contract," he said. "Tether and Circle can freeze, burn and reissue, which allows frozen USDT and USDC to be returned to a victim." But recovering bitcoin and ether is more challenging because they have no issuer that can directly freeze the assets. Instead, investigators must trace funds through exchanges and other crypto services where they can potentially be intercepted, added Redbord. Eric Jardine, head of research at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis, said returning frozen assets requires coordination among law enforcement, exchanges and token issuers. "There is no standard recovery timeline. A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC. Jardine added that while bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen by an issuer, they can still be traced and potentially recovered. Investigators can trace the funds on public blockchains and intervene when they reach a cooperating exchange or another centralized platform, he said. TRM Labs attributed the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit, based on on-chain and off-chain intelligence. The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights. TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance. The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes. TRM Labs said preparations for the attack began at least 36 hours before the theft, with the attackers using Tornado Cash, a cryptocurrency mixing service, to fund their wallets ahead of the breach. Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks. The attack does not currently appear to pose a significant solvency risk for Binance, according to Sean Farrell, head of digital asset strategy at Fundstrat Global Advisors. "The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said. Farrell estimated that around $3.3 billion in assets remained unfrozen. Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds. Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly. He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets. "I do not think that is the setup we are dealing with, but the key tell will be how quickly withdrawals resume and whether outflows stay orderly," Farrell said. The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton. Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable. "We need to make sure standards are incredibly high, but we have to really focus on the criminals," Perkins said. Perkins called for greater international cooperation to address cybersecurity threats, pointing to regulatory coordination among G20 countries following the global financial crisis as a potential model. He also said AI could help improve cybersecurity by identifying and addressing vulnerabilities, even as the technology is used by both attackers and defenders. Got a confidential news tip? extraction.body: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has reportedly suffered a major cyberattack, with hackers stealing cryptocurrencies worth $6.3 billion in what could be the biggest crypto heist in history. Confirming the incident, Binance said it was working to contain and resolve what it described as a "complex attack". The exchange said it was coordinating with law enforcement agencies and other industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen assets. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance wrote in a post on X. The exchange also cautioned that the estimated value of the stolen assets could rise further as investigations continue. The $6.3-billion figure may "continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," it said. Here's what we know about the reported Binance hack so far. What Happened? $6.3 Billion In Cryptocurrency Stolen According to Binance, around $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrencies were stolen from wallets used by the exchange to process transactions. In its initial assessment, the company believed the attack had originated from a compromised laptop. However, further investigation revealed additional security breaches. "However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance said. The attack targeted Binance.com, the exchange's global centralised platform. Binance.US, which serves customers in the United States, was not affected, the company said. Binance said the compromised laptop provided the attacker with access to a service container, enabling the submission of unauthorised withdrawal transactions. Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, described the incident as a "complex attack process". According to US-based blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs, the attackers compromised Binance's "signing infrastructure", which authorises transactions. This allegedly allowed them to issue instructions that drained the affected wallets. ALSO READ: Mohan Yadav Announces 2% DA Hike From January 2026 For MP Govt Employees Blockchain records indicate that the bulk of the heist took place within approximately 20 minutes. After moving the funds, the attackers attempted to transfer them beyond the reach of Binance's counterparties and stablecoin issuers. These entities have since frozen roughly half of the stolen assets. Binance and other authorities have not confirmed the identity of those responsible for the attack. However, US-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs has attributed the hack to a North Korean-linked group known as TraderTraitor, which it described as one of North Korea's elite hacking units. In a post on its website on Thursday, TRM said: "We make this judgment with high confidence." Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis also pointed towards the same group. Its co-founder and CEO, Jonathan Levin, wrote on X that the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK (North Korea) group TraderTraitor". Binance said on Friday that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds to manage the fallout from the attack. This includes $5 billion already held in the affected token assets. In an earlier statement, Teng said users' funds were safe. As a precautionary measure, the exchange also temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals. The company said it was working with its partners to freeze assets worth $3 billion that have been traced so far. However, freezing the assets does not necessarily mean they will be returned to Binance. It does, nevertheless, restrict the hackers' ability to convert the stolen cryptocurrencies into cash. Binance also said it remained on schedule to restore withdrawal services. "We are still on track towards the expected timeline to resume the withdrawal service in 45 hours," the exchange said. ALSO READ: Money Matters: Why Financial Conversations Remain Taboo In Indian Households

sources.title: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft - PBS
passages: Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation.
Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record.
Blockchain firms have pointed to the attack coming from a North Korean hacking unit.
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X.
Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said.
Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: "We're looking at that."
"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists."

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."
In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked.
The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.
Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets.
"Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines."
"We are working nonstop to resolve this," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X.
Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet.
"User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said.
"The vast majority sits in cold wallets" — which are offline and used for secure storage — "and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal."
Left: Binance logo and hacker code are seen in this illustration taken Oct.
Binance has said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two.

Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

The company said it has reserved more than $6.34 billion of company funds to cover the stolen assets and was beginning to recover assets for users. Binance worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. WATCH: $6 billion cryptocurrency heist puts investors on edge The cryptocurrency exchange has promised to cover all losses, and it has been sharing regular updates on its social media channels as it uncovers more information about the hack. "We are working nonstop to resolve this," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said Friday in a video posted to X. In an exchange Friday with reporters at the White House, President Donald Trump said U.S. officials were investigating the Binance hack. Asked whether North Korea was involved, Trump said: "We're looking at that." Here's what we know about the hack, possible North Korean involvement and Binance's investigation. Binance said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach." U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM, in a post on its website late Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said. "An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists." Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice." Experts have said that North Korea turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities in recent years as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties. In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets over the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the world's best. While about half of the stolen assets were frozen, there is evidence that the hackers already are transferring and converting some of what wasn't recovered, said Garrick Hileman, an independent cryptocurrency analyst. "Like in money laundering, you bring in the stolen goods and launder those through a mixer or tumbler," he said. "You mix it in with other cryptos, and it's harder to track." TRM and several other crypto firms and experts have said the hack represents the largest cryptocurrency theft on record. In February of last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack. TRM listed the Bybit hack when it referenced similarities between the Binance hack and previous attacks linked to TraderTraitor. Binance's founder, Changpeng Zhao, wrote on X that while Binance's hack might be the largest in terms of its dollar value, previous attacks on other companies like the crypto exchange Mt. Gox have had a more substantial impact in terms of the bitcoin amount affected, he said. Experts warn this scale of hacking could become more commonplace. "A cyber attack of this level is a matter of when, not if, particularly alongside the rise of AI," said Andy Ward, a senior vice president at Absolute Security. "Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated and widespread as ever, and it is likely only a matter of time before an even larger hack, with even greater financial fallout, makes headlines." The hack has raised questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, co-founder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab. "This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and that are connected to the internet. "User assets are held under Binance's established security architecture," he said. "The vast majority sits in cold wallets" — which are offline and used for secure storage — "and are only moved into a hot wallet when a user makes withdrawal." Teng said Binance's tech and security teams are "still deep" in investigating the hack. He said it was not carried out by one person and that the attackers used complex tactics, including a "self-destruct mechanism" that is making the incident more difficult to investigate. "We are working with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, token issuers and other exchanges to trace and recover stolen funds," Teng said. "We will do everything within our power to make sure that these bad actors will be held accountable."
