facts.text: Binance was hacked with an estimated impact of $6.3 billion, raising questions about the recovery of stolen funds and the broader fallout for crypto markets.
Around $3 billion in cryptocurrency assets have been frozen so far, according to a Binance security update .

Assuming frozen stablecoins are eventually returned, Binance's SAFU emergency fund, worth approximately $1.2 billion, could cover roughly a third of the remaining losses, with the balance coming from the exchange's own funds.

Chainalysis also pointed to North Korea , with co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin saying the firm assessed that the $6.4 billion Binance hack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor, citing links to previous attacks.
The firm estimated that approximately $6.36 billion in digital assets were moved from Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, with most transferred within about 20 minutes.
The FBI previously identified the same group as responsible for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, according to the company's insights.
"The most important takeaway for markets is that this does not currently appear to create meaningful solvency risk for Binance," Farrell said.

Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," Perkins said the industry must address cybersecurity challenges to reach its full potential, calling for stronger defenses and policies to hold cybercriminals accountable.
"A freeze stops the money from moving, and recovery follows through legal process," Redbord told CNBC.
A technical freeze may happen quickly, while returning funds can take months or years," Jardine told CNBC.
TRM Labs said the Binance attack shared characteristics with previous North Korea-linked incidents, including preparations made well before the theft and transaction signatures obtained in advance.
Farrell said the key indicators to watch were how quickly Binance resumes withdrawals and whether outflows remain orderly.
He added that a shortfall in customer assets could force the exchange to sell reserves, potentially triggering broader selling across crypto markets.
The Binance hack underscores the need for stronger cybersecurity standards and greater coordination among governments, according to Chris Perkins, head of Franklin Crypto at Franklin Templeton.

extraction.body: Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers. On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea. The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day. By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital. The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC. "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network." Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble. In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data. More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets. What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. "The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC. Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted. Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point. "We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options." GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin. "Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC. The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day. Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment. Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said. "Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. passages: Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers.
On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea.
The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day.
By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital.

The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC.
"Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."
Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble.

In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data.

More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets.

What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.

"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.
Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted.

Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.

"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options."
GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin.
"Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC.
The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day.

Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment.

Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.

"Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment."

extraction.body: Bitcoin has held up better than expected following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to Strive CEO Matt Cole, who said the breach does not undermine the cryptocurrency’s long-term investment thesis. Speaking on Cointelegraph’s Chain Reaction on Friday, Cole said the breach had not changed his long-term investment case for Bitcoin. He compared the attack on Binance’s wallets to a bank robbery rather than a failure of Bitcoin’s network. Bitcoin traded near $77,400 at 4:00 pm on Saturday, about 4% below its price shortly before the attack began Thursday, according to CoinGecko data. Strive, a publicly traded company that holds Bitcoin on its balance sheet, reported owning 43,000 BTC as of Oct. 23. “I do have conviction that over any reasonable time frame, this does not change the investment thesis on Bitcoin,” Cole said. Cole said Bitcoin’s decline was less severe than he expected given the scale of the breach and broader market weakness, although he acknowledged that it was too early to determine whether the cryptocurrency had reached a price bottom. Cole described the market as being in an “early spring” recovery phase that could last another six to nine months, with prices gradually rising rather than surging to new highs. Paul Chapman, financial crime director at Wirex, also distinguished the attack on Binance from a compromise of Bitcoin’s network. “It’s important to be clear that Bitcoin itself hasn’t been hacked — this was an attack on one company’s systems, not the network,” he told Cointelegraph. According to Glassnode, Thursday’s Binance breach was the largest cryptocurrency hack on record, with around $6.3 billion affected, exceeding the combined losses from the next nine largest hacks. The previous record was the $1.5 billion Bybit exploit in February 2025. Glassnode said three of the 10 largest crypto hacks have occurred since the beginning of 2025, all involving exchanges. Binance hack exceeds the next nine largest crypto exploits combined. Source: Glassnode By comparison, following the Bybit hack in 2025, Bitcoin fell roughly 5% from nearly $100,000 to around $95,000 amid the breach and broader market volatility, according to a Bitfinex market report. Anchorage Digital data cited by CNBC put Bitcoin’s average decline in the first 24 hours after previous crypto exchange exploits at 8.3%. Binance hack exposes exchange security vulnerabilities Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan said the attackers appeared to have compromised Binance’s transaction signing process. Binance said Friday that it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys, though its investigation remained ongoing. Blockaid’s analysis identified an Ethereum transaction containing 50 signed authorizations covering different transaction counts. A matching authorization allowed attacker-controlled code to operate through the wallet. Ben-Natan argued that checks before signing could have blocked the malicious authorization. extraction.body: Bitcoin slid to a six-week low on Friday, October 30, 2026, as traders weighed a Binance hack that the exchange put at roughly $6.3 billion. CNBC reported Bitcoin down 4.1% at $77,445.96, while CoinDesk tracked a dip toward $76,400 and a $1.57 billion liquidation wave across crypto futures. The Bitcoin Binance hack story now sits at the center of a week that also included a Federal Reserve hold and a heavy round of Big Tech earnings. The size of the theft is not the only reason the market flinched. Binance is the largest venue in crypto by most volume measures, so any sign that its withdrawal system was abused hits sentiment first and balance sheets second. Our earlier report on the laptop entry point covers how the attacker reportedly got in. This piece looks at the other side of the story, namely what the hack did to prices, leverage, fund flows and the next set of levels traders are watching. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Bitcoin entered the week near $80,000. We covered that level when the Fed held rates, in our note on Bitcoin at $80,100 after the Fed hold . The central bank kept its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4%, and two officials voted for a quarter-point increase, according to crypto.news. That split already made risk assets nervous before any Binance headline arrived. The first leg lower came on Thursday, October 29. Bitcoin Magazine described a drop below $79,000 as reports of the outflows spread, with a 24-hour range of $78,177.37 to $81,890 and a market cap near $1.58 trillion. By late Thursday evening The Block had Bitcoin below $77,000, trading at $76,664 as of 10 p.m. ET, down 4.5% over 24 hours. Friday brought the low. Forbes called it a six-week low, the weakest print since mid-September, with Bitcoin touching roughly $76,140 at the bottom. CoinDesk put the dip near $76,400, and Yahoo Finance reported Bitcoin recovering toward $77,300 for a 3% daily loss. Yahoo also noted Bitcoin was down about 7% for October. In other words, the hack did not start the slide, it sped it up. The pattern matters for how to read the move. A drop of 3% to 4.5% in a day is large by equity standards but ordinary for Bitcoin. A record theft at the biggest exchange produced a bruise, not a crash. Several analysts quoted below argued the same point. Two things stand out. First, ether and XRP fell more than Bitcoin, which fits a risk-off pattern where smaller assets carry more beta. Second, BNB dropped only 6% to 7%. The token tied most directly to the hacked company lost roughly what XRP lost, a sign that traders priced the event as a security scare and not as a solvency problem. Leverage did most of the damage. CoinDesk reported that crypto liquidations jumped fourfold to $1.57 billion after the hack hit prices. The Block counted $1.55 billion over 24 hours, and crypto.news counted $1.54 billion. Yahoo Finance put the figure at $1.6 billion. All four sit within a few percent of each other, so $1.5 billion to $1.6 billion is a safe range. Long positions took the brunt. The Block counted $1.34 billion in long liquidations out of $1.55 billion, crypto.news counted $1.30 billion, and Yahoo Finance counted $1.35 billion. Roughly 85% of the forced selling came from traders betting on higher prices. CoinDesk broke out Bitcoin at $468 million and ether at $358 million of the total. Trader counts ran between about 239,000 (crypto.news) and 246,482 (The Block). The single largest wipeout was an $11.09 million BTC/USDT position on Binance itself, per The Block and crypto.news. That is small next to the headline total. The flush came from a quarter of a million modest positions closing at once, not from a few whales. Liquidation cascades turn a 2% dip into a 4% dip. Exchanges close underwater longs with market sells, which pushes the price lower and trips the next batch of stops. Zeus Research analyst Dominick John told The Block that roughly $1.5 billion in 24-hour liquidations had added pressure on Bitcoin and ether. That is a mechanical effect. It fades once the weak leverage is gone, which is why many desks watch whether open interest resets after a flush like this one. The loss figure changed several times over two days. Binance itself estimated total impact near $6.3 billion and said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze about $3 billion. Independent trackers landed lower. The table lists the main numbers reported so far, and our piece on the gap between $5.7 billion and $2.54 billion frozen shows how the early estimates moved. Yahoo Finance listed the stolen assets by type. Bitcoin accounted for about $1.5 billion, ether about $900 million, USDT about $1.5 billion and USDC more than $800 million. That mix explains the price impact. The stolen Bitcoin is a modest slice of daily trading volume, while the stablecoin share is the part issuers can freeze. Whatever the final number, CoinDesk noted the incident surpasses the 2025 Bybit hack of about $1.5 billion, which was linked to North Korea. Bitcoin Magazine said the same, calling it the largest crypto theft on record if confirmed. The scale is roughly four times the Bybit loss on Binance’s own estimate. Stablecoin issuers acted within hours. CoinDesk reported that Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino froze $1.567 billion in USDT, and that Circle co-founder Jeremy Allaire froze more than $800 million in USDC. First Digital CEO Vincent Chok froze FDUSD as well. Bitcoin Magazine put the Circle figure near $823 million. Our explainer on who froze what walks through each issuer. Bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen that way. That is why analysts focus on the roughly $1.5 billion in stolen Bitcoin. ViaBTC analyst Jeff Ko told The Block that he does not expect the stolen Bitcoin to add significant selling pressure. The logic is simple. A thief who wants to cash out $1.5 billion of Bitcoin cannot do it in one day without wrecking the price they receive, and thieves of this class tend to move funds slowly through bridges and mixers. Binance moved fast on the balance-sheet question. Co-CEO Yi He pledged that the exchange will cover all user losses, per CNBC and The Block. Yahoo Finance reported that Binance reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds, and our walk-through of the $6.34 billion reserve math tests that number against the loss estimates. Former CEO Changpeng Zhao said he expects all user funds to be fully covered, according to Bitcoin Magazine. CNBC added that deposits at Binance were unaffected and the exchange expected withdrawals to resume within 48 hours. Binance.US confirmed it saw no impact, per Bitcoin Magazine. Those details did more to calm spot markets than any price level. The fear in a hack of this size is a bank-run dynamic, where users pull coins out at once and force the venue to sell assets into a falling market. A reserve larger than the highest loss estimate pushes that scenario down the probability list. Yahoo Finance reported that Binance also disclosed additional points of breach beyond the compromised engineer’s laptop it first suspected, without giving details. That keeps one question open. If the attacker had more than one door, the cleanup takes longer, and the withdrawal restart could slip. Traders will watch that timeline closely over the weekend. Fund flows told a calmer story than the price. According to crypto.news, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $17.07 million of net inflows on October 29, after $423.66 million over the prior three sessions. That is a small inflow on the day the hack broke, but it is still an inflow. Institutional holders did not run for the exits. Ether ETFs looked weaker, with $105 million of net withdrawals on the same day. The split fits the price action, where ether fell harder than Bitcoin. It also suggests allocators treat Bitcoin as the safer corner of the market when exchange risk spikes. If the attribution holds, the Bybit case offers a rough guide to behavior. CoinDesk linked the 2025 Bybit theft of about $1.5 billion to North Korea. Security researchers have long observed that groups of this type launder stolen ether and Bitcoin through chains of swaps and bridges over weeks, not hours. That slower pace is one reason some traders discount the risk of an immediate dump of the $1.5 billion in stolen Bitcoin. One related item came from our own coverage of a token tied to the heist. Shattered reported that the hacker dumped FUN and the token crashed 90% . That shows the attacker is willing to sell into thin markets, which keeps the dump risk alive for smaller assets even if Bitcoin itself holds. The shock traveled beyond Binance. CoinDesk reported that Polymarket suspended international trading and that $2.6 million had been drained from user accounts. That incident looks separate from the Binance theft but landed in the same news cycle. Our note on Polymarket resuming trading and repaying users follows how it ended. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said the company was doing everything it could to support Binance, according to The Block. That is an unusual note of cooperation between rivals. It reflects a shared interest in keeping the freeze network working and keeping retail confidence from sliding across the sector. Crypto has a long list of exchange breaches, and CNBC’s coverage reached back to two recent ones. Bybit lost about $1.5 billion in 2025, and Bitget lost $350 million. Binance’s incident is more than four times the Bybit loss on the company’s own estimate. The market digested those earlier events without a lasting trend change, which is why many traders treat hacks as short-lived volatility events. Still, size changes the calculus. A breach that touches the venue with the deepest liquidity raises questions about custody practices across the industry. Rival exchanges moved quickly to review their own controls, as we noted in our look at rivals tightening defenses . Pressure for fresh proof-of-reserve and key-management disclosures is a plausible next step, though no regulator has announced one in the reports we reviewed. For traders, the lesson is about leverage, not about direction. A quarter of a million positions closed in a day because many were stacked on the same side. Lower leverage, wider stops and attention to options expiry dates would have reduced the damage for most of them. For holders, the lesson is about custody. Binance says user deposits are unaffected and that it will cover losses, but a promise from any exchange is only as good as its balance sheet. Moving long-term holdings to self-custody removes that dependency. Our guide on hardware wallet security covers two failure modes and how to avoid them. Anyone who keeps funds on an exchange should enable withdrawal allowlists and watch official channels, since phishing messages spike after every major hack. For security teams, the reported entry point is the point to study. Binance’s own early findings pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave an attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals. CoinDesk noted that one transaction carried 50 wallet authorizations. Endpoint hygiene for privileged engineers, short-lived credentials and independent withdrawal approval are the controls that address that chain. CNBC reported Bitcoin down 4.1% to $77,445.96 on Friday, October 30. Forbes described a six-week low, with the intraday bottom near $76,140. Yahoo Finance reported Bitcoin down about 7% for October. Binance estimated total impact at about $6.3 billion. Chainalysis estimated about $5.9 billion, and Yahoo Finance reported $5.7 billion in stolen assets identified in attacker wallets. About $3 billion has been frozen, per Binance. Not on the data available. Crypto.news reported $17.07 million of net inflows into U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs on October 29, while Ether ETFs saw $105 million of net withdrawals. Bitcoin Magazine reported that Binance.US confirmed no impact on its platform. CNBC reported that deposits at Binance itself were unaffected. CNBC reported that Binance expected to resume withdrawals within 48 hours of its announcement. Yahoo Finance reported the exchange was working to restore the service. Check Binance’s official channels for the current status.

The Block counted $1.55 billion over 24 hours, and crypto.news counted $1.54 billion. Yahoo Finance put the figure at $1.6 billion. All four sit within a few percent of each other, so $1.5 billion to $1.6 billion is a safe range.

Long positions took the brunt. The Block counted $1.34 billion in long liquidations out of $1.55 billion, crypto.news counted $1.30 billion, and Yahoo Finance counted $1.35 billion. Roughly 85% of the forced selling came from traders betting on higher prices. CoinDesk broke out Bitcoin at $468 million and ether at $358 million of the total.

Trader counts ran between about 239,000 (crypto.news) and 246,482 (The Block). The single largest wipeout was an $11.09 million BTC/USDT position on Binance itself, per The Block and crypto.news. That is small next to the headline total. The flush came from a quarter of a million modest positions closing at once, not from a few whales.

Liquidation cascades turn a 2% dip into a 4% dip. Exchanges close underwater longs with market sells, which pushes the price lower and trips the next batch of stops. Zeus Research analyst Dominick John told The Block that roughly $1.5 billion in 24-hour liquidations had added pressure on Bitcoin and ether. That is a mechanical effect. It fades once the weak leverage is gone, which is why many desks watch whether open interest resets after a flush like this one.

The loss figure changed several times over two days. Binance itself estimated total impact near $6.3 billion and said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze about $3 billion. Independent trackers landed lower. The table lists the main numbers reported so far, and our piece on the gap between $5.7 billion and $2.54 billion frozen shows how the early estimates moved.

Yahoo Finance listed the stolen assets by type. Bitcoin accounted for about $1.5 billion, ether about $900 million, USDT about $1.5 billion and USDC more than $800 million. That mix explains the price impact. The stolen Bitcoin is a modest slice of daily trading volume, while the stablecoin share is the part issuers can freeze.

Whatever the final number, CoinDesk noted the incident surpasses the 2025 Bybit hack of about $1.5 billion, which was linked to North Korea. Bitcoin Magazine said the same, calling it the largest crypto theft on record if confirmed. The scale is roughly four times the Bybit loss on Binance’s own estimate.

Stablecoin issuers acted within hours. CoinDesk reported that Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino froze $1.567 billion in USDT, and that Circle co-founder Jeremy Allaire froze more than $800 million in USDC. First Digital CEO Vincent Chok froze FDUSD as well. Bitcoin Magazine put the Circle figure near $823 million. Our explainer on who froze what walks through each issuer.

Bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen that way. That is why analysts focus on the roughly $1.5 billion in stolen Bitcoin. ViaBTC analyst Jeff Ko told The Block that he does not expect the stolen Bitcoin to add significant selling pressure. The logic is simple. A thief who wants to cash out $1.5 billion of Bitcoin cannot do it in one day without wrecking the price they receive, and thieves of this class tend to move funds slowly through bridges and mixers.

Binance moved fast on the balance-sheet question. Co-CEO Yi He pledged that the exchange will cover all user losses, per CNBC and The Block. Yahoo Finance reported that Binance reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds, and our walk-through of the $6.34 billion reserve math tests that number against the loss estimates. Former CEO Changpeng Zhao said he expects all user funds to be fully covered, according to Bitcoin Magazine.

CNBC added that deposits at Binance were unaffected and the exchange expected withdrawals to resume within 48 hours. Binance.US confirmed it saw no impact, per Bitcoin Magazine. Those details did more to calm spot markets than any price level. The fear in a hack of this size is a bank-run dynamic, where users pull coins out at once and force the venue to sell assets into a falling market. A reserve larger than the highest loss estimate pushes that scenario down the probability list.

Yahoo Finance reported that Binance also disclosed additional points of breach beyond the compromised engineer’s laptop it first suspected, without giving details. That keeps one question open. If the attacker had more than one door, the cleanup takes longer, and the withdrawal restart could slip. Traders will watch that timeline closely over the weekend.

Fund flows told a calmer story than the price. According to crypto.news, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $17.07 million of net inflows on October 29, after $423.66 million over the prior three sessions. That is a small inflow on the day the hack broke, but it is still an inflow. Institutional holders did not run for the exits.

Ether ETFs looked weaker, with $105 million of net withdrawals on the same day. The split fits the price action, where ether fell harder than Bitcoin. It also suggests allocators treat Bitcoin as the safer corner of the market when exchange risk spikes.

If the attribution holds, the Bybit case offers a rough guide to behavior. CoinDesk linked the 2025 Bybit theft of about $1.5 billion to North Korea. Security researchers have long observed that groups of this type launder stolen ether and Bitcoin through chains of swaps and bridges over weeks, not hours. That slower pace is one reason some traders discount the risk of an immediate dump of the $1.5 billion in stolen Bitcoin.

One related item came from our own coverage of a token tied to the heist. Shattered reported that the hacker dumped FUN and the token crashed 90% . That shows the attacker is willing to sell into thin markets, which keeps the dump risk alive for smaller assets even if Bitcoin itself holds.

The shock traveled beyond Binance. CoinDesk reported that Polymarket suspended international trading and that $2.6 million had been drained from user accounts. That incident looks separate from the Binance theft but landed in the same news cycle. Our note on Polymarket resuming trading and repaying users follows how it ended.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said the company was doing everything it could to support Binance, according to The Block. That is an unusual note of cooperation between rivals. It reflects a shared interest in keeping the freeze network working and keeping retail confidence from sliding across the sector.

Crypto has a long list of exchange breaches, and CNBC’s coverage reached back to two recent ones. Bybit lost about $1.5 billion in 2025, and Bitget lost $350 million. Binance’s incident is more than four times the Bybit loss on the company’s own estimate. The market digested those earlier events without a lasting trend change, which is why many traders treat hacks as short-lived volatility events.

Still, size changes the calculus. A breach that touches the venue with the deepest liquidity raises questions about custody practices across the industry. Rival exchanges moved quickly to review their own controls, as we noted in our look at rivals tightening defenses . Pressure for fresh proof-of-reserve and key-management disclosures is a plausible next step, though no regulator has announced one in the reports we reviewed.

For traders, the lesson is about leverage, not about direction. A quarter of a million positions closed in a day because many were stacked on the same side. Lower leverage, wider stops and attention to options expiry dates would have reduced the damage for most of them.

For holders, the lesson is about custody. Binance says user deposits are unaffected and that it will cover losses, but a promise from any exchange is only as good as its balance sheet. Moving long-term holdings to self-custody removes that dependency. Our guide on hardware wallet security covers two failure modes and how to avoid them. Anyone who keeps funds on an exchange should enable withdrawal allowlists and watch official channels, since phishing messages spike after every major hack.

For security teams, the reported entry point is the point to study. Binance’s own early findings pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave an attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals. CoinDesk noted that one transaction carried 50 wallet authorizations. Endpoint hygiene for privileged engineers, short-lived credentials and independent withdrawal approval are the controls that address that chain.
CNBC reported Bitcoin down 4.1% to $77,445.96 on Friday, October 30. Forbes described a six-week low, with the intraday bottom near $76,140. Yahoo Finance reported Bitcoin down about 7% for October.

Binance estimated total impact at about $6.3 billion. Chainalysis estimated about $5.9 billion, and Yahoo Finance reported $5.7 billion in stolen assets identified in attacker wallets. About $3 billion has been frozen, per Binance.
Not on the data available. Crypto.news reported $17.07 million of net inflows into U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs on October 29, while Ether ETFs saw $105 million of net withdrawals.
Bitcoin Magazine reported that Binance.US confirmed no impact on its platform. CNBC reported that deposits at Binance itself were unaffected.

CNBC reported that Binance expected to resume withdrawals within 48 hours of its announcement. Yahoo Finance reported the exchange was working to restore the service. Check Binance’s official channels for the current status.

sources.title: Binance Hack: Why refunds alone won't solve crypto's security problem
passages: He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years.

Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach.

This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held.

This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks.

Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards.

The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes?

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

coreStoryFacts.text: "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC.
"This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."

"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.
Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers.

"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients.
The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin .
Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin.
Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events.
The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.
Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo.
That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.

Bitcoin has held up better than expected following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to Strive CEO Matt Cole, who said the breach does not undermine the cryptocurrency’s long-term investment thesis.
Paul Chapman, financial crime director at Wirex, also distinguished the attack on Binance from a compromise of Bitcoin’s network.
“It’s important to be clear that Bitcoin itself hasn’t been hacked — this was an attack on one company’s systems, not the network,” he told Cointelegraph.
Strive, a publicly traded company that holds Bitcoin on its balance sheet, reported owning 43,000 BTC as of Oct.
The previous record was the $1.5 billion Bybit exploit in February 2025.
Binance hack exceeds the next nine largest crypto exploits combined.
Binance hack exposes exchange security vulnerabilities
Bitcoin traded near $77,400 at 4:00 pm on Saturday, about 4% below its price shortly before the attack began Thursday, according to CoinGecko data.
Anchorage Digital data cited by CNBC put Bitcoin’s average decline in the first 24 hours after previous crypto exchange exploits at 8.3%.

extraction.body: Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers. On Thursday, the world's largest exchange by daily trading volume said that roughly $6.3 billion were affected in an exploit. Security firm TRM Labs linked the security incident to North Korea. The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin . On Friday, the cryptocurrency traded at $77,065 around 1:34 p.m. ET, down about 4% on the day. By comparison, the token has fallen 8.3% on average in the first 24 hours following past crypto exchange exploits, according to data from institutional crypto platform Anchorage Digital. The digital asset has remained relatively resilient because the hack on Binance had nothing to do with the security of the bitcoin network itself, according to Sam Callahan, director of bitcoin strategy and research at crypto treasury firm OranjeBTC. "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC. "This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network." Although Binance has suffered the largest hack in crypto history, it's far from the only digital asset exchange to fall victim to bad actors and lead bitcoin to tumble. In the early 2010s, bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin. The token fell as much as 23.7% in the first 24 hours after an attack on Mt. Gox in February 2014, per Anchorage Digital data. More recently, crypto exchange Bybit suffered roughly $1.5 billion in losses due to an exploit targeting its trading platform. Last month, crypto platform Bitget was drained of more than $350 million in digital assets. What's different about the Binance hack is that it hasn't sparked the same loss in confidence in crypto markets that occurred after other major crypto security incidents, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR. "The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC. Tether, Circle and several other crypto firms said they had frozen roughly $3 billion in funds stolen in the heist. That should help mitigate losses tied to the attack, the executive noted. Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events. The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point. "We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients. "ByBit also received a bridge loan after its $1.5bn hack last year; therefore, we believe Binance has financing options." GSR's Hallarn noted that this latest rotation out of technology stocks may also be to blame for some of the pressure on bitcoin. "Since the exploit, bitcoin has largely traded in lockstep with other risk assets, including equities, which sold off overnight amid concerns over AI-related earnings," Hallarn told CNBC. The iShares A.I. Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) was down more than 8% on the day. Still, Anchorage Digital head of research David Lawant noted that current holders of bitcoin are more likely to hold their tokens through short-term headwinds than holders of other risk-on assets at the moment. Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo. That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said. "Bitcoin and crypto are not these hot-topic [assets like tech stocks] that investors are fleeing in and out," Lawant said. "The current holder base is a pretty strong one that is able to look at these things with a slightly longer-term view. That's playing a big role in how bitcoin is behaving well in this negative market environment." extraction.body: Bitcoin has held up better than expected following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to Strive CEO Matt Cole, who said the breach does not undermine the cryptocurrency’s long-term investment thesis. Speaking on Cointelegraph’s Chain Reaction on Friday, Cole said the breach had not changed his long-term investment case for Bitcoin. He compared the attack on Binance’s wallets to a bank robbery rather than a failure of Bitcoin’s network. Bitcoin traded near $77,400 at 4:00 pm on Saturday, about 4% below its price shortly before the attack began Thursday, according to CoinGecko data. Strive, a publicly traded company that holds Bitcoin on its balance sheet, reported owning 43,000 BTC as of Oct. 23. “I do have conviction that over any reasonable time frame, this does not change the investment thesis on Bitcoin,” Cole said. Cole said Bitcoin’s decline was less severe than he expected given the scale of the breach and broader market weakness, although he acknowledged that it was too early to determine whether the cryptocurrency had reached a price bottom. Cole described the market as being in an “early spring” recovery phase that could last another six to nine months, with prices gradually rising rather than surging to new highs. Paul Chapman, financial crime director at Wirex, also distinguished the attack on Binance from a compromise of Bitcoin’s network. “It’s important to be clear that Bitcoin itself hasn’t been hacked — this was an attack on one company’s systems, not the network,” he told Cointelegraph. According to Glassnode, Thursday’s Binance breach was the largest cryptocurrency hack on record, with around $6.3 billion affected, exceeding the combined losses from the next nine largest hacks. The previous record was the $1.5 billion Bybit exploit in February 2025. Glassnode said three of the 10 largest crypto hacks have occurred since the beginning of 2025, all involving exchanges. Binance hack exceeds the next nine largest crypto exploits combined. Source: Glassnode By comparison, following the Bybit hack in 2025, Bitcoin fell roughly 5% from nearly $100,000 to around $95,000 amid the breach and broader market volatility, according to a Bitfinex market report. Anchorage Digital data cited by CNBC put Bitcoin’s average decline in the first 24 hours after previous crypto exchange exploits at 8.3%. Binance hack exposes exchange security vulnerabilities Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan said the attackers appeared to have compromised Binance’s transaction signing process. Binance said Friday that it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys, though its investigation remained ongoing. Blockaid’s analysis identified an Ethereum transaction containing 50 signed authorizations covering different transaction counts. extraction.body: Bitcoin slid to a six-week low on Friday, October 30, 2026, as traders weighed a Binance hack that the exchange put at roughly $6.3 billion. CNBC reported Bitcoin down 4.1% at $77,445.96, while CoinDesk tracked a dip toward $76,400 and a $1.57 billion liquidation wave across crypto futures. The Bitcoin Binance hack story now sits at the center of a week that also included a Federal Reserve hold and a heavy round of Big Tech earnings. The size of the theft is not the only reason the market flinched. Binance is the largest venue in crypto by most volume measures, so any sign that its withdrawal system was abused hits sentiment first and balance sheets second. Our earlier report on the laptop entry point covers how the attacker reportedly got in. This piece looks at the other side of the story, namely what the hack did to prices, leverage, fund flows and the next set of levels traders are watching. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Bitcoin entered the week near $80,000. We covered that level when the Fed held rates, in our note on Bitcoin at $80,100 after the Fed hold . The central bank kept its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4%, and two officials voted for a quarter-point increase, according to crypto.news. That split already made risk assets nervous before any Binance headline arrived. The first leg lower came on Thursday, October 29. Bitcoin Magazine described a drop below $79,000 as reports of the outflows spread, with a 24-hour range of $78,177.37 to $81,890 and a market cap near $1.58 trillion. By late Thursday evening The Block had Bitcoin below $77,000, trading at $76,664 as of 10 p.m. ET, down 4.5% over 24 hours. Friday brought the low. Forbes called it a six-week low, the weakest print since mid-September, with Bitcoin touching roughly $76,140 at the bottom. CoinDesk put the dip near $76,400, and Yahoo Finance reported Bitcoin recovering toward $77,300 for a 3% daily loss. Yahoo also noted Bitcoin was down about 7% for October. In other words, the hack did not start the slide, it sped it up. The pattern matters for how to read the move. A drop of 3% to 4.5% in a day is large by equity standards but ordinary for Bitcoin. A record theft at the biggest exchange produced a bruise, not a crash. Several analysts quoted below argued the same point. Two things stand out. First, ether and XRP fell more than Bitcoin, which fits a risk-off pattern where smaller assets carry more beta. Second, BNB dropped only 6% to 7%. The token tied most directly to the hacked company lost roughly what XRP lost, a sign that traders priced the event as a security scare and not as a solvency problem. Leverage did most of the damage. CoinDesk reported that crypto liquidations jumped fourfold to $1.57 billion after the hack hit prices. The Block counted $1.55 billion over 24 hours, and crypto.news counted $1.54 billion. Yahoo Finance put the figure at $1.6 billion. All four sit within a few percent of each other, so $1.5 billion to $1.6 billion is a safe range. Long positions took the brunt. The Block counted $1.34 billion in long liquidations out of $1.55 billion, crypto.news counted $1.30 billion, and Yahoo Finance counted $1.35 billion. Roughly 85% of the forced selling came from traders betting on higher prices. CoinDesk broke out Bitcoin at $468 million and ether at $358 million of the total. Trader counts ran between about 239,000 (crypto.news) and 246,482 (The Block). The single largest wipeout was an $11.09 million BTC/USDT position on Binance itself, per The Block and crypto.news. That is small next to the headline total. The flush came from a quarter of a million modest positions closing at once, not from a few whales. Liquidation cascades turn a 2% dip into a 4% dip. Exchanges close underwater longs with market sells, which pushes the price lower and trips the next batch of stops. Zeus Research analyst Dominick John told The Block that roughly $1.5 billion in 24-hour liquidations had added pressure on Bitcoin and ether. That is a mechanical effect. It fades once the weak leverage is gone, which is why many desks watch whether open interest resets after a flush like this one. The loss figure changed several times over two days. Binance itself estimated total impact near $6.3 billion and said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze about $3 billion. Independent trackers landed lower. The table lists the main numbers reported so far, and our piece on the gap between $5.7 billion and $2.54 billion frozen shows how the early estimates moved. Yahoo Finance listed the stolen assets by type. Bitcoin accounted for about $1.5 billion, ether about $900 million, USDT about $1.5 billion and USDC more than $800 million. That mix explains the price impact. The stolen Bitcoin is a modest slice of daily trading volume, while the stablecoin share is the part issuers can freeze. Whatever the final number, CoinDesk noted the incident surpasses the 2025 Bybit hack of about $1.5 billion, which was linked to North Korea. Bitcoin Magazine said the same, calling it the largest crypto theft on record if confirmed. The scale is roughly four times the Bybit loss on Binance’s own estimate. Stablecoin issuers acted within hours. CoinDesk reported that Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino froze $1.567 billion in USDT, and that Circle co-founder Jeremy Allaire froze more than $800 million in USDC. First Digital CEO Vincent Chok froze FDUSD as well. Bitcoin Magazine put the Circle figure near $823 million. Our explainer on who froze what walks through each issuer. Bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen that way. That is why analysts focus on the roughly $1.5 billion in stolen Bitcoin. ViaBTC analyst Jeff Ko told The Block that he does not expect the stolen Bitcoin to add significant selling pressure. The logic is simple. A thief who wants to cash out $1.5 billion of Bitcoin cannot do it in one day without wrecking the price they receive, and thieves of this class tend to move funds slowly through bridges and mixers. Binance moved fast on the balance-sheet question. Co-CEO Yi He pledged that the exchange will cover all user losses, per CNBC and The Block. Yahoo Finance reported that Binance reserved more than $6.34 billion in company funds, and our walk-through of the $6.34 billion reserve math tests that number against the loss estimates. Former CEO Changpeng Zhao said he expects all user funds to be fully covered, according to Bitcoin Magazine. CNBC added that deposits at Binance were unaffected and the exchange expected withdrawals to resume within 48 hours. Binance.US confirmed it saw no impact, per Bitcoin Magazine. Those details did more to calm spot markets than any price level. The fear in a hack of this size is a bank-run dynamic, where users pull coins out at once and force the venue to sell assets into a falling market. A reserve larger than the highest loss estimate pushes that scenario down the probability list. Yahoo Finance reported that Binance also disclosed additional points of breach beyond the compromised engineer’s laptop it first suspected, without giving details. That keeps one question open. If the attacker had more than one door, the cleanup takes longer, and the withdrawal restart could slip. Traders will watch that timeline closely over the weekend. Fund flows told a calmer story than the price. According to crypto.news, U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $17.07 million of net inflows on October 29, after $423.66 million over the prior three sessions. That is a small inflow on the day the hack broke, but it is still an inflow. Institutional holders did not run for the exits. Ether ETFs looked weaker, with $105 million of net withdrawals on the same day. The split fits the price action, where ether fell harder than Bitcoin. It also suggests allocators treat Bitcoin as the safer corner of the market when exchange risk spikes. If the attribution holds, the Bybit case offers a rough guide to behavior. CoinDesk linked the 2025 Bybit theft of about $1.5 billion to North Korea. Security researchers have long observed that groups of this type launder stolen ether and Bitcoin through chains of swaps and bridges over weeks, not hours. That slower pace is one reason some traders discount the risk of an immediate dump of the $1.5 billion in stolen Bitcoin. One related item came from our own coverage of a token tied to the heist. Shattered reported that the hacker dumped FUN and the token crashed 90% . That shows the attacker is willing to sell into thin markets, which keeps the dump risk alive for smaller assets even if Bitcoin itself holds. The shock traveled beyond Binance. CoinDesk reported that Polymarket suspended international trading and that $2.6 million had been drained from user accounts. That incident looks separate from the Binance theft but landed in the same news cycle. Our note on Polymarket resuming trading and repaying users follows how it ended. Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said the company was doing everything it could to support Binance, according to The Block. That is an unusual note of cooperation between rivals. It reflects a shared interest in keeping the freeze network working and keeping retail confidence from sliding across the sector. Crypto has a long list of exchange breaches, and CNBC’s coverage reached back to two recent ones. Bybit lost about $1.5 billion in 2025, and Bitget lost $350 million. Binance’s incident is more than four times the Bybit loss on the company’s own estimate. The market digested those earlier events without a lasting trend change, which is why many traders treat hacks as short-lived volatility events. Still, size changes the calculus. A breach that touches the venue with the deepest liquidity raises questions about custody practices across the industry. Rival exchanges moved quickly to review their own controls, as we noted in our look at rivals tightening defenses . Pressure for fresh proof-of-reserve and key-management disclosures is a plausible next step, though no regulator has announced one in the reports we reviewed. For traders, the lesson is about leverage, not about direction. A quarter of a million positions closed in a day because many were stacked on the same side. Lower leverage, wider stops and attention to options expiry dates would have reduced the damage for most of them. For holders, the lesson is about custody. Binance says user deposits are unaffected and that it will cover losses, but a promise from any exchange is only as good as its balance sheet. Moving long-term holdings to self-custody removes that dependency. Our guide on hardware wallet security covers two failure modes and how to avoid them. Anyone who keeps funds on an exchange should enable withdrawal allowlists and watch official channels, since phishing messages spike after every major hack. For security teams, the reported entry point is the point to study. Binance’s own early findings pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave an attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals. CoinDesk noted that one transaction carried 50 wallet authorizations. Endpoint hygiene for privileged engineers, short-lived credentials and independent withdrawal approval are the controls that address that chain. CNBC reported Bitcoin down 4.1% to $77,445.96 on Friday, October 30. Forbes described a six-week low, with the intraday bottom near $76,140. Yahoo Finance reported Bitcoin down about 7% for October. Binance estimated total impact at about $6.3 billion. Chainalysis estimated about $5.9 billion, and Yahoo Finance reported $5.7 billion in stolen assets identified in attacker wallets. About $3 billion has been frozen, per Binance. Not on the data available. Crypto.news reported $17.07 million of net inflows into U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs on October 29, while Ether ETFs saw $105 million of net withdrawals. Bitcoin Magazine reported that Binance.US confirmed no impact on its platform. CNBC reported that deposits at Binance itself were unaffected. CNBC reported that Binance expected to resume withdrawals within 48 hours of its announcement. Yahoo Finance reported the exchange was working to restore the service. Check Binance’s official channels for the current status.

The market digested those earlier events without a lasting trend change, which is why many traders treat hacks as short-lived volatility events.

Still, size changes the calculus. A breach that touches the venue with the deepest liquidity raises questions about custody practices across the industry. Rival exchanges moved quickly to review their own controls, as we noted in our look at rivals tightening defenses . Pressure for fresh proof-of-reserve and key-management disclosures is a plausible next step, though no regulator has announced one in the reports we reviewed.

For traders, the lesson is about leverage, not about direction. A quarter of a million positions closed in a day because many were stacked on the same side. Lower leverage, wider stops and attention to options expiry dates would have reduced the damage for most of them.

For holders, the lesson is about custody. Binance says user deposits are unaffected and that it will cover losses, but a promise from any exchange is only as good as its balance sheet. Moving long-term holdings to self-custody removes that dependency. Our guide on hardware wallet security covers two failure modes and how to avoid them. Anyone who keeps funds on an exchange should enable withdrawal allowlists and watch official channels, since phishing messages spike after every major hack.

For security teams, the reported entry point is the point to study. Binance’s own early findings pointed to a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop that gave an attacker access to a service container, which was then used to submit unauthorized withdrawals. CoinDesk noted that one transaction carried 50 wallet authorizations. Endpoint hygiene for privileged engineers, short-lived credentials and independent withdrawal approval are the controls that address that chain.
CNBC reported Bitcoin down 4.1% to $77,445.96 on Friday, October 30. Forbes described a six-week low, with the intraday bottom near $76,140. Yahoo Finance reported Bitcoin down about 7% for October.

Binance estimated total impact at about $6.3 billion. Chainalysis estimated about $5.9 billion, and Yahoo Finance reported $5.7 billion in stolen assets identified in attacker wallets. About $3 billion has been frozen, per Binance.
Not on the data available. Crypto.news reported $17.07 million of net inflows into U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs on October 29, while Ether ETFs saw $105 million of net withdrawals.
Bitcoin Magazine reported that Binance.US confirmed no impact on its platform. CNBC reported that deposits at Binance itself were unaffected.

CNBC reported that Binance expected to resume withdrawals within 48 hours of its announcement. Yahoo Finance reported the exchange was working to restore the service. Check Binance’s official channels for the current status.

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.
