facts.text: "Investors recognize an important distinction: Bitcoin itself was not hacked," Callahan told CNBC.
"This was a security breach at a centralized exchange, not a failure of the Bitcoin network."

"The speed of Binance's response, its deep financial resources, and its assurances that no user funds would be lost have helped restore market confidence and prevent potential panic," Hallarn told CNBC.
Binance has suffered the biggest hack in crypto history , but that's done little to shake confidence in bitcoin , according to market analysts and researchers.

"We believe Binance has more than enough liquidity to cover the hole and we expect the exchange to remain solvent while reimbursing user funds," Compass Point analyst Ed Engel said Friday in a note to clients.
The hack sparked a slight sell-off in bitcoin .
Gox was hacked a handful of times, wreaking havoc on the price of bitcoin.
Binance also has a $1.2 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users to offset losses from security breaches and other events.
The firm could also be eligible for loans that would minimize its solvency risks, if history is any indication, according to investment bank Compass Point.
Binance said it has started recovering affected assets, which has likely assuaged some of investors' concerns, according to Spencer Hallarn, head of markets at crypto trading firm GSR.
Just 6% of bitcoin is held in exchange-traded funds, according to data from bitcoin analytics platform Bitbo.
That suggests many bitcoins are still being held by long-term believers in the asset and its cypherpunk origins, Lawant said.

Bitcoin has held up better than expected following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, according to Strive CEO Matt Cole, who said the breach does not undermine the cryptocurrency’s long-term investment thesis.
Paul Chapman, financial crime director at Wirex, also distinguished the attack on Binance from a compromise of Bitcoin’s network.
“It’s important to be clear that Bitcoin itself hasn’t been hacked — this was an attack on one company’s systems, not the network,” he told Cointelegraph.
Strive, a publicly traded company that holds Bitcoin on its balance sheet, reported owning 43,000 BTC as of Oct.

extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, experienced a record $6.3 billion security exploit this week Dan Kitwood / Getty Images Crypto exchange Binance said Saturday it has been able to replace 90% of the amount stolen after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform that the FBI blamed on North Korea. Binance said it was able to replace the funds taken in the record hack by using company money to buy new tokens. The remaining 10% consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. Crypto prices fell Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe. The FBI on Saturday said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Teng said Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals Sunday. Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT Saturday, as part of its proof-of-reserves process. Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.

passages: Federal Bureau of Investigation has officially confirmed that North Korea was behind the $6.3 billion (about 8.4 trillion won) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
The North Korea-linked hacking group disabled the exchange's security systems in just 20 minutes and siphoned off the funds, while Binance could only watch without taking meaningful action.

extraction.body: Federal Bureau of Investigation has officially confirmed that North Korea was behind the $6.3 billion (about 8.4 trillion won) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange. The North Korea-linked hacking group disabled the exchange's security systems in just 20 minutes and siphoned off the funds, while Binance could only watch without taking meaningful action. "We are announcing that North Korea was behind the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance," the FBI said on the 31st. It was the first time the FBI has officially identified North Korea as being behind a hack. The FBI said the perpetrator was TraderTraitor, known as one of North Korea's elite hacking groups, and that the stolen assets were seen being converted mainly into Ethereum. The agency expects further laundering as the cryptocurrency is swapped for other digital assets through decentralized finance platforms and instant exchange services. "A hack at the world's largest exchange means security spending alone does not guarantee safety," said Hwang Suk-jin, a professor at Dongguk University's Graduate School of Information Security. "A similar incident could happen in South Korea."

sources.title: FBI says North Korea behind $6 billion crypto theft from Binance
passages: New York: The FBI on Saturday accused North Korea of stealing more than $6 billion in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance in what is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist.The US law enforcement agency's statement came as Binance offered reassurances it was covering the losses from the hacking attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 percent of what was stolen.Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes.

The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea -- which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programs -- to find illicit means to capture revenue.TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said in its latest update they were on track to resume Sunday.The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.Bitcoin plunged nearly five percent after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly six percent and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent.Binance said Friday it was working to resolve what it called a complex attack with several points of breach.

extraction.body: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, experienced a record $6.3 billion security exploit this week Dan Kitwood / Getty Images Crypto exchange Binance said Saturday it has been able to replace 90% of the amount stolen after a $6.3 billion hack of its platform that the FBI blamed on North Korea. Binance said it was able to replace the funds taken in the record hack by using company money to buy new tokens. The remaining 10% consists of tokens that are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, it said in a statement posted on X. "We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," co-CEO Richard Teng said on X. Crypto prices fell Friday, while Binance — the world's biggest crypto exchange — sought to reassure customers that their funds were safe. The FBI on Saturday said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Members of the unit were observed by law enforcement converting stolen assets into the cryptocurrency ethereum, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expects "further laundering" of the assets through the use of related technology. Teng said Friday that the breach was a "complex attack" involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate. After the hack, the exchange stopped allowing customers to withdraw their funds, but it said Saturday it was still on track to reopen withdrawals Sunday. Binance said it has set aside around $6.34 billion of company funds internally to cover the losses. The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1 billion Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company's own corporate treasury, it said on X. Binance also said it had taken a new snapshot of assets held on its platform as of 0000 GMT Saturday, as part of its proof-of-reserves process. Users holding the 10 listed tokens — BTC, ETH, USDT, BNB, SOL, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD, and ZEC — would be able to verify that their assets were backed at a minimum ratio of 1:1 once the full proof was available, it said.

sources.title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety - CNBC
passages: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. passages: He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years.

Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach.

This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held.

This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks.

Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards.

The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes?

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

passages: The $6.3 billion theft from Binance raises alarms over future cyber threats, experts warn.
Founder Changpeng Zhao acknowledged the breach and thanked other cryptocurrency companies for assisting in freezing affected assets.
Udaipur Kiran was first established in 2006 as a weekly newspaper.
After successfully publishing the newspaper for a few years, it became evident that its reach was limited.
To expand its audience, Udaipur Kiran launched its website in 2013.

Initially, the website was introduced under the domain name udaipurkiran.com and primarily catered to English-speaking readers.Read Local News Over time, based on reader demand, Udaipur Kiran expanded its offerings by launching a Hindi version of the website, named udaipurkiran.org.
Bhupendra Singh Chundawat is a seasoned technology journalist with over 22 years of experience in the media industry.
He specializes in covering the global technology landscape, with a deep focus on manufacturing trends and the geopolitical impact on tech companies.
Currently serving as the Editor at Udaipur Kiran , his insights are shaped by decades of hands-on reporting and editorial leadership in the fast-evolving world of technology.
In response to the hack, Binance set aside over $6.34 billion of its own funds to cover losses, with $5 billion already in the stolen cryptocurrencies.
Binance confirmed that its internet-connected cryptocurrency wallets were accessed, allowing unauthorized withdrawals of significant amounts.

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion theft from Binance raises alarms over future cyber threats, experts warn. NEW DELHI, Oct 31: Hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion in digital assets from Binance, one of the largest thefts in financial history. coreStoryFacts.text: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years.

Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach.

This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held.

This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks.

Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards.

The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes?

Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents . Most of these experts even said that observers should expect more security incidents, at least in the near term, as that problem worsens. "I think it's extremely dangerous," said Tyler Moore, a cybersecurity professor at the University of Tulsa who has followed the asset class for more than a decade. "I think you should be very wary of leaving any significant amount of funds in an exchange… there are no built-in protections for when these inevitable hacks take place." For instance, banking customers can rely on the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to insure deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, in the event of an institution's failure. There is no similar form of coverage available for funds lost from a cryptocurrency exchange, noted Moore. Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole. That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid. "I actually think no users will lose any money," he said. "Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges. These exchanges need to work really hard to make sure they don't take another hit like this." Ben-Natan noted that while he thinks more hacks are likely as the cybersecurity landscape changes due to AI, he said it will only make the crypto industry stronger. As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said. A key point is that while Binance experienced a security incident on its offshore platform, its regulated, centralized U.S. exchange did not have a similar issue. The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange. U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath. In a Friday appearance on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator of derivatives — Chairman Michael Selig said that the offshore nature of these incidents was critical to note. "They don't have the same sorts of safeguards that we have in our financial markets," he said. "We want to offer a federal option to these exchanges to come and register with the CFTC, and they would be subject to the same sorts of cybersecurity safeguards that we have in our markets today." Brett Falk, a professor and director of the Crypto and Society Lab at the University of Pennsylvania, said that U.S. regulations likely wouldn't have stopped an incident like that of Binance on Thursday. That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X . "Most of the regulation doesn't touch the specific software stack you have to use to authenticate people," Falk said. In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were. Falk echoed the argument by Ben-Natan that individuals likely won't face losses, and that it's better for traders to leave funds with an exchange where they have the financial backing of a company rather than in a self-custody wallet where no one can refund their losses in the event of a hack. Ben-Natan added that traders should feel secure based on how many incidents companies like his catch that don't become news. That's because the security technology often works and stops them before they become major incidents. However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC. That's because of how much liquidity individuals can quickly access in the event of a successful breach. It's why Ryan Kirkley, CEO of blockchain infrastructure company Global Settlement Network, thinks traders should be cautious leaving their funds in any wallet that's not backed by insurance until financial companies upgrade their security infrastructure. "I do not think there's anything right now that is a common solution in the marketplace where your assets are truly safe," Kirkley said. "Unless you are dealing with a reputable and firm broker-dealer that provides an asset insurance, you are risking your assets putting them into any ecosystem today just simply because there's so much unknown," he added. passages: He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years.

Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach.

This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held.

This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks.

Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards.

The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes?

extraction.body: The $6.3 billion security breach at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, has renewed concerns about the safety of digital assets and the risks of keeping investments on centralised trading platforms. While the exchange has pledged to cover all losses and around $3 billion worth of assets have reportedly been frozen, the incident raises a larger question: how can crypto platforms prevent such attacks rather than simply compensate investors after a breach?Binance's preliminary investigation has pointed to a possible compromise of a developer engineer's laptop, which may have allowed an attacker to access an internal service and initiate unauthorised withdrawals. The incident highlights the risks associated with internal access to systems handling large amounts of digital assets.Vineet Budki, Partner and CEO of Sigma Capital, believes the solution lies in stronger security measures, better industry cooperation and greater investor awareness.In an interview with CNBC-TV18, Budki said cyberattacks were not new to the digital world, but the growing use of online platforms for financial transactions had increased the potential consequences of a security breach. He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years. Web 3 has taken this further by allowing people to transact through digital platforms.This has increased the financial stakes involved in cyberattacks."Anything that involves a transaction carries the risk of being hacked," Budki said.He pointed to incidents such as the theft of $80 million from the Bank of Bangladesh in 2016 and the Mt. Gox and WazirX hacks to underline that security breaches are not unique to any one segment of the digital economy.The Binance incident also raises questions about the security of internal systems. If an employee's compromised device can provide access to services that authorise transactions, exchanges need to ensure that such access cannot be exploited to move large amounts of assets.According to Budki, technology will continue to improve, but attackers will also find new ways to exploit vulnerabilities. This makes security an ongoing challenge for platforms handling digital transactions.What should crypto investors do to protect their assets?The Binance breach also highlights why investors should not concentrate their cryptocurrency holdings on a single exchange.Budki said risk diversification should extend beyond the choice of asset classes to include how digital assets are held. Investors should consider their overall exposure to crypto alongside investments in real estate, gold and other assets.He also advised against keeping all cryptocurrency holdings on one trading platform. Instead, investors should consider splitting their holdings between exchanges and private wallets.This brings self-custody into focus. Unlike assets held on an exchange, cryptocurrency stored in a private wallet gives investors greater control over how their holdings are accessed and transferred."Not your wallet, not your money," Budki said.His point is that investors who leave their assets on an exchange depend on the platform's security systems and controls. Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach. While Budki believes such a commitment can restore confidence in the founder, he does not see compensation as a long-term answer to the industry's security challenges.A founder's ability to reimburse investors can provide reassurance, particularly when the exchange has sufficient financial resources. However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards. This could include a dedicated body to develop solutions against hacking groups such as the Lazarus Group, which has been linked to attacks on several exchanges.The objective should be to establish stronger preventive mechanisms so that exchanges are better equipped to identify threats and stop attacks before they result in substantial losses.What security measures should crypto exchanges strengthen?Budki believes exchanges need multiple layers of security, backed by independent oversight and continuous monitoring.He identified third-party security audits as an important measure and suggested that exchanges could also explore using banks as custodians to strengthen the protection of digital assets.Another critical area is the management of hot and cold wallets.Cold wallets are not connected to the internet and are therefore less exposed to online attacks. Hot wallets, by contrast, are accessible through the internet and are needed to facilitate transactions.Since exchanges need to maintain some assets in hot wallets to process withdrawals and other transactions, securing these systems is particularly important.Budki said exchanges should deploy multiple security solutions and have independent teams monitoring their systems around the clock. The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes? Could it have been stopped in under one minute?" he asked.Can the crypto industry prevent stolen funds from moving?Security measures within individual exchanges are only part of the solution. Budki believes companies across the cryptocurrency ecosystem also need to work together to restrict the movement of stolen assets after a breach.He pointed to the response by Tether and Circle, which froze cryptocurrency worth hundreds of millions of dollars following the incident, as an example of what industry cooperation can achieve.Such coordination could help limit the movement of stolen funds, although the same approach is not possible with every cryptocurrency. Budki noted that freezing assets such as Bitcoin and Ethereum is not possible in the same way.He believes exchanges, stablecoin issuers and other industry participants need to work towards more effective ways of responding to attacks.Budki also suggested exploring insurance products for cryptocurrency deposits, with large providers potentially offering protection against losses arising from security breaches.For the industry, the challenge is to move beyond relying on individual exchanges to deal with attacks after they happen. Stronger internal security, faster responses and cooperation between market participants will be essential to reducing the risks faced by investors.The Binance breach may be followed by compensation for affected users, but Budki's argument is that lasting confidence in crypto platforms will depend on their ability to prevent such incidents in the first place.Watch accompanying video for full conversation.

sources.title: Binance Loses $6.3 Billion in Hack, Experts Warn of Rising Cyber Threats - Udaipur Kiran
passages: The $6.3 billion theft from Binance raises alarms over future cyber threats, experts warn.
Founder Changpeng Zhao acknowledged the breach and thanked other cryptocurrency companies for assisting in freezing affected assets.
Udaipur Kiran was first established in 2006 as a weekly newspaper.
After successfully publishing the newspaper for a few years, it became evident that its reach was limited.
To expand its audience, Udaipur Kiran launched its website in 2013.

Initially, the website was introduced under the domain name udaipurkiran.com and primarily catered to English-speaking readers.Read Local News Over time, based on reader demand, Udaipur Kiran expanded its offerings by launching a Hindi version of the website, named udaipurkiran.org.
Bhupendra Singh Chundawat is a seasoned technology journalist with over 22 years of experience in the media industry.
He specializes in covering the global technology landscape, with a deep focus on manufacturing trends and the geopolitical impact on tech companies.
Currently serving as the Editor at Udaipur Kiran , his insights are shaped by decades of hands-on reporting and editorial leadership in the fast-evolving world of technology.
In response to the hack, Binance set aside over $6.34 billion of its own funds to cover losses, with $5 billion already in the stolen cryptocurrencies.

story.title: Binance’s $6.3 billion hack raises questions about crypto wallet safety - CNBC

facts.text: A security incident at digital asset exchange Binance on Thursday affected some $6.3 billion in client assets, making it the largest crypto theft on record.
Experts whom CNBC interviewed said the security incidents on the crypto exchanges aren't surprising, especially in light of recent artificial intelligence hacking incidents .
That's because the hack may have involved a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, Binance said in a post on X .
Two high-profile security breaches this week – including the biggest cryptocurrency theft in history – are raising questions on the safety of storing funds in a wallet on a crypto exchange .
Binance and Polymarket reassured users that they would make affected investors whole.
That's a sign that users should feel confident in crypto exchanges, according to Ido Ben-Natan , CEO of blockchain security company Blockaid.
"I actually think no users will lose any money," he said.
"Binance has said they're going to cover everything… I actually don't think it's a bad idea for users to put money in these exchanges.
As a result, a crypto wallet could ultimately become a safer place to hold funds compared to other options, since the industry will have the experience of how to handle these attacks, Ben-Natan said.
However, crypto may be a unique target for hackers in a changing cybersecurity landscape, these experts told CNBC.

Earlier that day, prediction market platform Polymarket temporarily halted trading on its international exchange after a third-party data provider was hacked, resulting in at least $2.7 million being drained from users' wallets.
The same was true of Polymarket's domestic exchange.
U.S. regulated platforms Coinbase and Robinhood were also unaffected by the security breach on Binance, though shares of both fell on Friday in the aftermath.
In another social media post, BInance later said its investigation uncovered additional points of breach , though the company didn't specify what they were.

He also emphasised that investors and exchanges need to rethink how crypto assets are stored and protected.Here is what the Binance hack tells us about the vulnerabilities of crypto platforms and the measures needed to address them.Why are crypto exchanges vulnerable to hacks?Budki believes crypto hacks are part of a wider cybersecurity problem that has affected internet platforms and financial institutions for years.

Even established exchanges with substantial security resources can face breaches, making it important for investors to avoid relying entirely on a single custodian.Why refunding investors is not enoughBinance has pledged to cover the losses arising from the breach.

However, returning money after a hack does not address the weaknesses that allowed the breach to happen.Budki compared this with the banking system, where the focus should be on strengthening institutions and scrutinising their processes rather than relying on refunds after a collapse.He believes the cryptocurrency industry needs similar safeguards.

The speed at which funds can be moved during an attack makes the ability to detect suspicious activity and respond quickly crucial.Referring to the Binance breach, in which most of the funds were reportedly moved within about 20 minutes, he questioned whether better monitoring could have stopped the attack much earlier."Could it have been stopped in five minutes?

extraction.body: Suspected North Korean hackers hit Binance for US$6.3 billion. Photo / Getty Images Hackers pilfered US$6.3 billion from the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange in a stunning attack that halted withdrawals on the platform and set off a race among digital currency companies to freeze billions in stolen funds. The main thrust of the attack on Binance took about 20 minutes, according to third-party cyber security firms who examined public flows of cryptocurrency in and out of the exchange. It remains unclear how the hackers managed to breach the systems of Binance to steal the US$6.3b ($11.1b). At least two firms have attributed the hack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state hacker group that has been behind other major crypto thefts, based in part on analysis of the flow of funds. Binance has not said who it thinks is responsible. Binance said on Thursday (local time) that its initial investigation pointed to the compromise of one engineer’s laptop as the source of the hack. The company has since said it thinks there were additional breaches in the attack. “This was a complex attack,” Richard Teng, the exchange’s CEO, said in a video on social media. “The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate.” The heist was breathtaking not only for its scope but for its speed, with billions of funds vanishing in only minutes. Cryptocurrency, which runs on a decentralised exchange called blockchain, is supposed to be able to move quickly by design. “This is not just the biggest hack in crypto. It’s actually the biggest hack in the world, ever,” Ido Ben-Natan, the chief executive of crypto security company Blockaid, said. According to cyber security firm CrowdStrike, a US$1.5b theft in 2025 from the exchange Bybit – also a cryptocurrency hack eventually attributed to North Korean attackers – was previously the largest single financial theft ever reported. Some details of the attack, including how the hackers got inside Binance, are still unclear. But because cryptocurrency runs on a decentralised network, all transactions are public. In the hours after the heist, a number of crypto research firms scrambled to trace the apparent flow of funds out of Binance into other cryptocurrency accounts, known in the industry as wallets. At least three companies have released reports detailing their analysis of what happened. The US$6.3b theft from Binance kicked off an apparent cat-and-mouse game where the hackers rushed to split the stolen money up among various wallets, according to third-party analysts, knowing that cryptocurrency issuers would attempt to freeze the funds. The blockchain security company Chainalysis said in a blog post that the volume of transactions suggested that the attackers relied on automated activity to “obscure the trail of funds” by quickly shuffling money in and out of various wallets. The hackers appeared to swipe funds in a variety of cryptocurrencies, some of them centrally issued by companies, who rushed to lock down hundreds of millions in assets on Binance. Within about an hour, the companies Circle and Tether had frozen about US$971 million and $825 million in their respective stablecoins – a kind of digital dollar that is pegged to a secure asset such as the US dollar. Binance has since said that about US$3b of the stolen funds were frozen by various partners, preventing the hackers from transferring them further. But the traditional model of cryptocurrencies, like bitcoin, live out in the wild on completely decentralised networks where it’s not possible to pull the plug. TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company, said it observed the hackers racing to convert their loot into these non-freezable cryptocurrencies, by seeking out loan platforms or “market-makers” that would make the switch. In all, at least US$2.4b appears to be “beyond any issuer’s reach”, TRM Labs said. Binance has said it will refund customers through a combination of its own funds and a US$1b bitcoin reserve designed to cover hacking incidents and other emergencies. The exchange has paused withdrawals while it conducts security checks. The hack comes during heightened fears of cyber attacks enabled by powerful artificial intelligence systems. While it’s not clear that the Binance hackers used artificial intelligence (AI), cryptocurrency is a fast-moving industry where “they’re basically building the plane as they’re flying it” Benjamin Cole, a professor at Fordham University, said. “Basically across every endpoint on the internet at this point – companies of every stripe, be they crypto or not – there’s a growing sense that there is a new cyber security reality in play,” Eric Jardine, the head of research at Chainalysis, said. The hack underscores several characteristics of cryptocurrency, envisioned by enthusiasts as a liberating substitute for the traditional financial system. Instead of banks and governments managing accounts and regulating currencies, cryptocurrency can move from user to user in a decentralised manner. And despite efforts to move cryptocurrency into the mainstream, those characteristics have made the technology an attractive opportunity for criminals, terrorist groups and other actors who might otherwise be barred from banks. While Binance has not said who it thinks is responsible for the hack, two cyber security firms attribute it to TraderTraitor. Chainalysis, one of the firms, said it observed money stolen from Binance co-mingling with funds from a US$388m heist of a different cryptocurrency exchange last month that was also attributed to North Korean attackers. In all, TRM Labs estimates that North Korean hackers have stolen US$12.8b in cryptocurrency over more than 100 incidents since 2017 (the country’s estimated domestic gross product in 2025 was about US$26b). TraderTraitor has been identified as the cause for previous major crypto hacks, including the US$1.5b theft from Bybit. That heist, too, was executed in only minutes. Binance has faced a number of legal issues. In 2023, its chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, pleaded guilty to violating criminal anti-money-laundering guidelines meant to prevent illicit transactions. The company also pleaded guilty to criminal charges after prosecutors accused it of allowing transactions from al-Qaeda, the Islamic State, Hamas and other groups. Binance said at the time it took responsibility “for this past chapter”. Zhao, who stepped down as chief executive, was pardoned by US President Donald Trump, whose Administration said the crypto executive was unfairly targeted by the Biden Administration. The company was also fined US$4.3b. Binance has no official headquarters and was founded in China in 2017. Binance.US, its American version, said it was not affected. Binance said it is co-ordinating with global law enforcement and several US agencies said they were aware of the hack or investigating it. “Secret Service investigators are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday,” Secret Service spokesman Thomas Lynch said in a statement. The Secret Service, in addition to protecting the president, also investigates cyber crimes. But even with some funds recovered, the hack appears to be a record-setting heist. “With a couple hundred elite hackers, they’re far exceeding the revenues of the things North Korea used to sell,” Nick Carlsen, an investigator at TRM Labs, said of TraderTraitor. “This is just basically the North Korean Government’s primary source of hard currency revenue now.”

Hackers pilfered US$6.3 billion from the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange in a stunning attack that halted withdrawals on the platform and set off a race among digital currency companies to freeze billions in stolen funds.
The main thrust of the attack on Binance took about 20 minutes, according to third-party cyber security firms who examined public flows of cryptocurrency in and out of the exchange.

It remains unclear how the hackers managed to breach the systems of Binance to steal the US$6.3b ($11.1b). At least two firms have attributed the hack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state hacker group that has been behind other major crypto thefts, based in part on analysis of the flow of funds. Binance has not said who it thinks is responsible.

Binance said on Thursday (local time) that its initial investigation pointed to the compromise of one engineer’s laptop as the source of the hack. The company has since said it thinks there were additional breaches in the attack.

“This was a complex attack,” Richard Teng, the exchange’s CEO, said in a video on social media. “The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and traces as they went, making it more difficult for us to trace and investigate.”

The heist was breathtaking not only for its scope but for its speed, with billions of funds vanishing in only minutes. Cryptocurrency, which runs on a decentralised exchange called blockchain, is supposed to be able to move quickly by design.
“This is not just the biggest hack in crypto. It’s actually the biggest hack in the world, ever,” Ido Ben-Natan, the chief executive of crypto security company Blockaid, said.

According to cyber security firm CrowdStrike, a US$1.5b theft in 2025 from the exchange Bybit – also a cryptocurrency hack eventually attributed to North Korean attackers – was previously the largest single financial theft ever reported.

Some details of the attack, including how the hackers got inside Binance, are still unclear. But because cryptocurrency runs on a decentralised network, all transactions are public. In the hours after the heist, a number of crypto research firms scrambled to trace the apparent flow of funds out of Binance into other cryptocurrency accounts, known in the industry as wallets. At least three companies have released reports detailing their analysis of what happened.

The US$6.3b theft from Binance kicked off an apparent cat-and-mouse game where the hackers rushed to split the stolen money up among various wallets, according to third-party analysts, knowing that cryptocurrency issuers would attempt to freeze the funds.

The blockchain security company Chainalysis said in a blog post that the volume of transactions suggested that the attackers relied on automated activity to “obscure the trail of funds” by quickly shuffling money in and out of various wallets.

The hackers appeared to swipe funds in a variety of cryptocurrencies, some of them centrally issued by companies, who rushed to lock down hundreds of millions in assets on Binance. Within about an hour, the companies Circle and Tether had frozen about US$971 million and $825 million in their respective stablecoins – a kind of digital dollar that is pegged to a secure asset such as the US dollar.
Binance has since said that about US$3b of the stolen funds were frozen by various partners, preventing the hackers from transferring them further.

But the traditional model of cryptocurrencies, like bitcoin, live out in the wild on completely decentralised networks where it’s not possible to pull the plug. TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company, said it observed the hackers racing to convert their loot into these non-freezable cryptocurrencies, by seeking out loan platforms or “market-makers” that would make the switch.
In all, at least US$2.4b appears to be “beyond any issuer’s reach”, TRM Labs said.
Binance has said it will refund customers through a combination of its own funds and a US$1b bitcoin reserve designed to cover hacking incidents and other emergencies.
The exchange has paused withdrawals while it conducts security checks.

The hack comes during heightened fears of cyber attacks enabled by powerful artificial intelligence systems. While it’s not clear that the Binance hackers used artificial intelligence (AI), cryptocurrency is a fast-moving industry where “they’re basically building the plane as they’re flying it” Benjamin Cole, a professor at Fordham University, said.

“Basically across every endpoint on the internet at this point – companies of every stripe, be they crypto or not – there’s a growing sense that there is a new cyber security reality in play,” Eric Jardine, the head of research at Chainalysis, said.

The hack underscores several characteristics of cryptocurrency, envisioned by enthusiasts as a liberating substitute for the traditional financial system. Instead of banks and governments managing accounts and regulating currencies, cryptocurrency can move from user to user in a decentralised manner.

And despite efforts to move cryptocurrency into the mainstream, those characteristics have made the technology an attractive opportunity for criminals, terrorist groups and other actors who might otherwise be barred from banks.

While Binance has not said who it thinks is responsible for the hack, two cyber security firms attribute it to TraderTraitor. Chainalysis, one of the firms, said it observed money stolen from Binance co-mingling with funds from a US$388m heist of a different cryptocurrency exchange last month that was also attributed to North Korean attackers.

In all, TRM Labs estimates that North Korean hackers have stolen US$12.8b in cryptocurrency over more than 100 incidents since 2017 (the country’s estimated domestic gross product in 2025 was about US$26b). TraderTraitor has been identified as the cause for previous major crypto hacks, including the US$1.5b theft from Bybit. That heist, too, was executed in only minutes.

Binance has faced a number of legal issues. In 2023, its chief executive, Changpeng Zhao, pleaded guilty to violating criminal anti-money-laundering guidelines meant to prevent illicit transactions. The company also pleaded guilty to criminal charges after prosecutors accused it of allowing transactions from al-Qaeda, the Islamic State, Hamas and other groups. Binance said at the time it took responsibility “for this past chapter”.

Zhao, who stepped down as chief executive, was pardoned by US President Donald Trump, whose Administration said the crypto executive was unfairly targeted by the Biden Administration. The company was also fined US$4.3b.
Binance has no official headquarters and was founded in China in 2017. Binance.US, its American version, said it was not affected.
Binance said it is co-ordinating with global law enforcement and several US agencies said they were aware of the hack or investigating it.

“Secret Service investigators are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle, to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday,” Secret Service spokesman Thomas Lynch said in a statement. The Secret Service, in addition to protecting the president, also investigates cyber crimes.
But even with some funds recovered, the hack appears to be a record-setting heist.

“With a couple hundred elite hackers, they’re far exceeding the revenues of the things North Korea used to sell,” Nick Carlsen, an investigator at TRM Labs, said of TraderTraitor. “This is just basically the North Korean Government’s primary source of hard currency revenue now.”

Binance has not said who it thinks is responsible. Binance said on Thursday (local time) that its initial investigation pointed to the compromise of one engineer’s laptop as the source of the hack. According to cyber security firm CrowdStrike, a US$1.5b theft in 2025 from the exchange Bybit – also a cryptocurrency hack eventually attributed to North Korean attackers – was previously the largest single financial theft ever reported. Some details of the attack, including how the hackers got inside Binance, are still unclear. But because cryptocurrency runs on a decentralised network, all transactions are public. In the hours after the heist, a number of crypto research firms scrambled to trace the apparent flow of funds out of Binance into other cryptocurrency accounts, known in the industry as wallets. At least three companies have released reports detailing their analysis of what happened. The US$6.3b theft from Binance kicked off an apparent cat-and-mouse game where the hackers rushed to split the stolen money up among various wallets, according to third-party analysts, knowing that cryptocurrency issuers would attempt to freeze the funds. The blockchain security company Chainalysis said in a blog post that the volume of transactions suggested that the attackers relied on automated activity to “obscure the trail of funds” by quickly shuffling money in and out of various wallets. The hackers appeared to swipe funds in a variety of cryptocurrencies, some of them centrally issued by companies, who rushed to lock down hundreds of millions in assets on Binance. Within about an hour, the companies Circle and Tether had frozen about US$971 million and $825 million in their respective stablecoins – a kind of digital dollar that is pegged to a secure asset such as the US dollar. Binance has since said that about US$3b of the stolen funds were frozen by various partners, preventing the hackers from transferring them further. But the traditional model of cryptocurrencies, like bitcoin, live out in the wild on completely decentralised networks where it’s not possible to pull the plug. TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence company, said it observed the hackers racing to convert their loot into these non-freezable cryptocurrencies, by seeking out loan platforms or “market-makers” that would make the switch. In all, at least US$2.4b appears to be “beyond any issuer’s reach”, TRM Labs said. Instead of banks and governments managing accounts and regulating currencies, cryptocurrency can move from user to user in a decentralised manner. And despite efforts to move cryptocurrency into the mainstream, those characteristics have made the technology an attractive opportunity for criminals, terrorist groups and other actors who might otherwise be barred from banks. While Binance has not said who it thinks is responsible for the hack, two cyber security firms attribute it to TraderTraitor. Chainalysis, one of the firms, said it observed money stolen from Binance co-mingling with funds from a US$388m heist of a different cryptocurrency exchange last month that was also attributed to North Korean attackers. The Secret Service, in addition to protecting the president, also investigates cyber crimes. extraction.body: Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has started to allow its customers to withdraw their funds from the platform, as it recovers from a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack. The exchange was hit by the theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit. Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach, but on Sunday announced that it had began a phased reopening after 2pm Singapore time. The first phase will allow people who hold the ethereum, USDT and USDC tokens on the ethereum blockchain to withdraw their funds, as well as some others held on the BNB Smart Chain blockchain. The platform said it has replenished 90% of the ⁠amount stolen. The remaining 10% of tokens are less liquid, meaning they ⁠may take ​longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday. Richard Teng, Binance’s co-chief executive, said separately that the company was “committed to covering the ⁠remaining 10%” and that users would not bear the financial impact of the hack. It came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack. TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un. “The Federal Bureau of Investigation is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6bn in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement. The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services. It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors” were “using to launder these stolen assets”. Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it ‌harder to trace and investigate. Binance said it had set aside around $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses. “Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said. The money spent rebuying tokens came from using part of its $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some ⁠of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said ​on X. The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols. Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%. The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.
